summary: Great Growth Opportunities, but Work-Life Balance Comes at a Cost
pros: Strong opportunities for advancement and leadership development. You can gain experience across multiple areas of the business, lead large teams, develop associates, and learn a great deal about operations. Benefits and bonus potential can also be good.
cons: Work-life balance can be extremely difficult for salaried management. Long days, six-day workweeks, and working on scheduled days off can become common when a facility is struggling or understaffed. Expectations and accountability are high, but compensation and recognition do not always feel proportionate to the additional workload or responsibilities. Your overall experience can also depend heavily on the support and leadership style of store and market-level management.
advice: Invest more consistently in retaining experienced leaders, not just developing replacements. When salaried managers repeatedly take on additional hours, responsibilities, and operational challenges, recognize that contribution through meaningful compensation, staffing support, and career development. Leadership should also place greater emphasis on sustainable work-life balance and consistent support from upper management.

summary: Strong Employees, but Poor Management Accountability
pros: Smart coworkers, strong benefits, challenging work, and opportunities to learn.
cons: In my experience, management quality was highly inconsistent and accountability often felt one-sided. Work-life balance was poor, with frequent escalations, changing priorities, nights, and weekends. Performance decisions could feel subjective, with visibility and management relationships sometimes carrying too much weight. After more than a decade at Amazon, my separation experience also left me feeling that long tenure and past contributions carried little weight.
advice: Invest in real leadership training before placing people in management roles. Strong individual performance does not automatically translate into the ability to lead, coach, develop, and retain a team. New managers should receive structured training in people leadership, performance management, communication, conflict resolution, and employee development rather than being expected to learn through trial and error. Hold managers to the same standards of accountability expected of employees, create more consistency in performance decisions, and recognize when poor management is driving burnout or attrition.

summary: Frustrating sales goals and communication issues hinder success
pros: The interactions with other associates is wonderful. The care, associate to associate is nice. Store manager is compassionate
cons:
1. Managers do not communicate with each other. As a sales specialist, you can have a work plan for attaining the “goals” (money you should bring in per week, per month, per quarter, per year.) but on a daily basis you are asked to go to a different area of the store to do special projects, taking you off the specialty floor so that you aren’t getting those sales. The specialists who are not asked to do special projects snag the sales. Not a good system. 

2. Have scanners at each specialty station. If you ask us to ring up customers with baskets of items, follow your own SOP and have scanners at each station. I was told it is too expensive to order more. It is MORE time-consuming for the customer, causing a bad customer experience. I’ve also lost sales of  items we stock like bathtubs, microwave ovens, and freezers because a customer just wants to go through a register up front and get out of the store, and the process of asking for all of their information in order-up then having to scan the barcode of other items with our first phone, then entering the SKU by hand into the system, takes FAR too long. (And the name of the game here is CUSTOMER SERVICE.) hmmm. 

3. As a specialist with a monetary “goal,” any time a customer returns an appliance for any reason, or if the delivery team damages, scratches, or dings a product, that money is deducted from my goal. We don’t make COMMISSION, so why would that money be taken off of my goal? I did my job by spending time with the customer, arranging the delivery, setting up a credit card, and possibly selling an extended warranty. I put in the time and closed the sale. Wouldn’t that be why we have “goals?” To make sure we are closing sales? There are times we spend an hour or more with customers, only to have an appliance or specialty item returned because of a delivery issue that we have no control of. Fix this system. It is the biggest source of frustration to specialists on Viva Engage.

4. Then there are new specialty bosses that come in and treat “goals” like “quotas.” Asking us to go over to the other end of the store and check out Pro customers who have a phone sale, in order to make our “goal” number. Knowing full well that this goal number that we reach will make her/him look good, so they can move up in management. It isn’t that we closed loads of new sales in our respective specialty areas, we have simply moved a number (sale) from a cashier, to our personal specialist number, gaming the system. No NEW BUSINESS was done, in fact, because I’m out of my specialty area, I could have lost sales. It’s simply moving numbers around, and treating your employees like interchangeable pieces on a crazy board game of numbers. Numbers are not metrics. Metrics actually measure something. 

Closing thoghts: Aldi stores have people who do all jobs during their shifts, but they pay those people for that. If THD wants to follow that model, they need to pay people to do that, and better yet put it in the job description, and offer comprehensive training for that. Comprehensive training would look like doing a rotation in a specific specialty area, alongside a mentor or seasoned specialist in that specific area for a given amount of time, like 4-6 weeks to really learn the area.
advice:
Require managers on duty to have daily meetings and communicate special tasks that need doing. No specialist needs 3 managers telling them 3 different tasks that take them away from their primary function and goals. 

Decide how important customer service is, and offer tools for your employees that actually HELP to achieve customer service goals. Order-up is not a good tool, not having scanners at each workstation does not help customers, taking away credit for sales, when the work has been done and the return has zero to do with the effort of the salesperson-BAD policy. 

Goals that are treated like quotas, and threats of write-ups if goals aren’t met- You will lose good employees. I can say with honesty that I know you have.

Specialty managers (SASM) who promote the model of going into other specialty areas and poaching sales, for instance, Millwork coming into flooring, when a flooring associate is right there, maybe at the other end of the aisle, and not handing the customer off, are harming a culture of teamwork. Don’t cultivate that kind of “me first” culture. It’s happening and it’s not part of The Home Depot’s culture. 

THD, you can do better at the store level. I absolutely love my supervisor. Above him/her it gets a bit chaotic with communication. Managers talk about your shifts amongst yourselves before jumping on the floor with assignments, and give space to employees who have been on the floor all day.

summary: The Home Depot — A Deeply Disappointing and Toxic Work Environment
pros: Sometimes there's food in the break room for certain events.
cons:
Management: Management is the biggest issue I have experienced. Employees are constantly monitored and made to feel as though anything they say or do can potentially be used against them. There have been instances of managers watching employees from the ends of aisles, creating an atmosphere where simply talking while working can be interpreted as not working.
Extreme stress and pressure: The constant scrutiny, threats of write-ups, and fear of termination have created an extremely stressful work environment. Personally, this job has affected my sleep and overall physical and mental well-being.
Breaks don't always feel like breaks: Employees have reportedly had their photographs taken by management while asleep in the break room during their breaks, allegedly as evidence for disciplinary action. Regardless of management's reasoning, this feels invasive and contributes to the feeling that employees are never truly off the clock.
Severe understaffing: There have been weeks with approximately 500–600 project hours but only around 272 employee hours available. Employees are expected to somehow make up the difference despite not having enough people to realistically complete the workload.
Poor attitude toward staffing: Instead of addressing staffing shortages, employees have been told things such as, “I'd rather have no help than bad help.” Comments like this make employees feel disposable rather than valued.
Toxic division between departments: MET, store-side, and overnight employees all work for the same company, yet employees have been encouraged to view themselves as separate teams and told that they will eventually dislike one another. This creates unnecessary tension and makes it harder for employees to work together.
District management: There appears to be an excessive emphasis on finding reasons to discipline or terminate employees rather than helping them succeed. Employees can feel threatened with write-ups or termination for briefly stopping to ask questions or clarify something.
Questionable disciplinary decisions: There was an incident in which a district manager apparently mistook one employee for another and nearly attempted to fire the wrong person. When someone's livelihood is at stake, mistakes like that are extremely concerning.
Heat and working conditions: During periods when temperatures outside have reached approximately 110°F, employees have struggled with inadequate air conditioning. Employees have also been warned against attempting to adjust the thermostat themselves, even in the break room, under threat of disciplinary action.
Attendance and scheduling inconsistencies: Employees are told about the company's clock-in grace period but are simultaneously expected to arrive several minutes early so they can be working exactly at their scheduled start time. Employees can then be questioned about overtime that results from these expectations.
Hours being used as punishment: Employees have reported having their hours reduced after calling out, with comments suggesting that employees who don't show up don't need the hours. This creates the impression that scheduling is being used as a form of punishment.
Very little hands-on training: Training consists heavily of videos rather than actual hands-on instruction. When employees have questions, they may be met with frustration instead of guidance, leaving many employees to teach themselves.
Employees are discouraged from seeking help: Many employees end up learning from store-side associates because they aren't receiving adequate training, yet they can then get in trouble for interacting with those same associates. This puts employees in an impossible position.
Employee morale: The combination of understaffing, constant monitoring, unrealistic expectations, disciplinary threats, and lack of support has created extremely low morale.
Mental and physical health: The level of stress has taken a serious toll on some employees. People have discussed unhealthy ways of coping with the pressure, and I have personally heard employees discuss severe mental-health struggles, including suicidal thoughts. That should be an enormous red flag for any company.
Overall culture: The biggest problem is that employees frequently feel like productivity numbers and company interests matter more than the people actually doing the work.
advice: Start listening to your employees instead of constantly looking for reasons to discipline them. Provide adequate staffing, meaningful hands-on training, reasonable workloads, and a safe working environment. Stop treating employees like numbers and start treating them like people. If management spent as much effort supporting employees as it does monitoring and threatening them, morale and productivity would likely improve significantly.

summary: Terrible work environment with constant threats and stress
pros: No pros at all at this job. DO NOT APPLY
cons: Horrendous place to work. Store locations have tons of theft. They add the job of security guard to your job description but won’t train or pay you for it. When you try to catch someone by calling the manager, you are told “not much I can do about that.” So then why are we told to inform management of theft if you won’t do anything. If you don’t inform then it’s a write up. You are expected to do unreasonable amounts of work in a short time frame or else you will be written up. Speaking of write ups, if you enjoy those then you will love this place because every mistake is a write up. Dont finish a task? Write up. Did a task the wrong way or simply forgot to do it? Write up. Work too slowly? Write up. Take the bus and show up a couple mins late? Write up. Didn’t take a required lunch break because you had too much to do? Write up. This place is terrible. Fear based work place and very stressful. Every manager I talked to was very short with me and rude. Came off as fake when they were trying to look nice. Like icing on a plastic cupcake. They don’t have benefits for working there. They do but you have to pay for the benefits which isn’t a benefit. It’s giving money back to the company that paid you. Healthcare, Dental, Vision, Insurance none of it is paid for by the company. You want to be covered for something they will be happy to charge you. Need some shopping done while at work? How about 15 percent off all Walgreens brand items only. Sounds good until you realize thats it’s really a dollar here and there youre saving which isn’t much. I haven’t even touched the schedule yet. Flexible schedule it says? Nope. I asked off during the interview for Sundays off due to my faith. I was told yes. Worked every single Sunday and hardly made it to church because they had me close every Saturday night. Told them I bus so by the time we lock up at 10pm I am not home until 11 and a shower, brush teeth etc not in bed until 11:45 but WAIT CHURCH IS AT 6AM.. yeah can’t make it to church. Talked to them about and they said the same thing “Maybe next schedule” days off you have to schedule WAY in advance which is insane because life happens in weeks so you can’t schedule anything. They don’t care about you are your family either, I missed the final moments of my grandfather passing. I called to tell them I won’t make it to work due to my grandfather passing away. I was told find someone to cover your shift or you will be fired. WOW Im losing a family member and you threaten me with losing my livelihood as well? Fantastic. Same thing when I hurt my foot and my back unloading a truck. I asked for it to be recorded and I need to fill out a worker’s comp form. I was told NO and then was expected to get back to work. Searing pain and was hard to move but if I didn’t then I lost my job. These people seem to want to write you up, yell at you and make life difficult more than help you out and make you a strong part of the company. I NEVER got properly trained. The GM was supposed to train me and months in I STILL didn’t know how to do things. summary: Unethical practices overshadow decent pay for pharmacists
pros: I do not understand if the positive reviews are dependent on location or if pharmacists are too afraid to stand up for ourselves. The only positive aspect of being a former employee of Kroger was the pay but our once decent annual raises have become a thing of the past.
cons: Our benefits are not great for the simple fact that how are we offered mid plans as healthcare providers ourselves. The new CEO is not good for this company having been a former private equity investor… Kroger has become so focused on metrics and now, offer vaccines this past July, which I did not recommend to anyone unless under serious circumstances like immunocompromised patients. Even then, money and the shareholders who hold all the power have no liability in their business decisions that we have to learn and are expected to follow. Frankly, this company has become so unethical that I could not fathom being a pharmacist here nor being proud to have worked there. I am actually embarrassed. Additionally, just look how the managers are making schedules for their own technicians… metrics people. That’s illegal in my state, but it is it like this is the first time Kroger has conducted illegal practices and procedures. Look up their current lawsuit about the Kroger Savings Program. Honestly, I could go on about this once good company but I will not waste any more energy on pharmacists that took an oath to protect our patients and do no harm.. etc., yet I feel as though it may be Opposite Day everyday when I worked there. Truly a disgrace and all these organizations want to talk about provider status but I disagree until pharmacy personnel are actually kept up on practice guidelines, stop playing the high school political games, have some respect for others and yourselves (not everyone but many), and the most frustrating statement I would internally cringe at is that patients are referred to as customers but patients are not customers. Thanks for listening to my personal opinions, respectfully.
advice: Stay up to date on pharmacy jurisprudence and the practice of being clinically competent in the practice. Listen to your employees because in my area before I left, there were so many pharmacists that left the company and many were posting for pharmacy managers. The technicians need to get a serious pay raise for the fact that they are a huge aspect and assets to a solid team. You all are running everyone out so bad that there’s so many technicians who float, which when I started and before this new CEO took over, never did I see or even think there were floater technicians. That says so much about what is the most important aspect of what you want out of your career. Where did morality, ethical values, and team building while rewarding employees for consistently showing up every shift and going beyond (which isn’t even possible with the workload which should have provided more incentive **pay your employees **). Good luck to all who are still hanging on strong, I hope your experiences will continue to be positive for you and wish everyone success in their future, truly.

pros: It's not a constant go go go. There are short periods of downtime.
cons: Everything else seems to be bad at the moment.  There have been several rounds of small, quiet layoffs (enough to keep everyone in a constant state of discomfort). Although we may know WHERE we're trying to head to, the constant organizational and leadership changes we're being subject to create so much chaos and confusion that nobody knows HOW we can accomplish any of our goals. There are strict processes for everything, with highly detailed and structured systems to prioritize the company's work, but inevitably everything becomes a priority since management does not respect the overly complicated processes they make the rest of us follow. They can come in as they please and blow up any kind of work prioritization that may have been in place.
advice: Stop being a bunch of grifters that are milking the company dry. Value your employees, their knowledge and expertise. The founder always put people first and FedEx used to care about its employees, but now everyone is just a number on a spreadsheet. Execs need to stop looking for short term wins to fatten their paychecks. Making major changes every 4 to 6 months in the name of "streamlining" the organization is highly disruptive and does not give anyone a chance to settle into the new environment, develop new relationships, build knowledge and ways of working. It's like having a new job every 4 to 6 months!

Work assignments and yearly high performance ratings are arranged accordingly, with limited connection to the actual scope of work or performance.
- The harder you work, the more work you get. You are expected to take over more and more tasks until you are exhausted. There is little work-life balance, with frequent early-morning and late-night meetings. Yet working harder does not necessarily lead to a higher rating or promotion. When you try to discuss and manage your workload with your manager, you may receive negative reviews.
- Bullying among colleagues. Some colleagues, especially more senior ones, bully their peers in ways similar to how they treat OEMs, including publicly criticizing colleagues for non-work-related reasons and being uncooperative at work. Leaders generally tolerate this behavior and may even give negative teamwork feedback to those being bullied.
advice: Allow transparency in the performance review and promotion process. Treat employees fairly and more like human beings, rather than just tools.

summary: A once-great culture diminished by corporate greed and AI focus
pros:
When I joined, the company offered generous bonuses, an inclusive environment, and a genuinely positive culture. Engineers and managers were engaged, and it felt like a place where people truly wanted to work. Over time, however, significant changes, including the focus on corporate growth and the race to develop AI, have transformed that experience, and much of what made the company special is no longer present.

That said, the role is a good fit for people who enjoy constant change and learning new things, as there is always something new to work on. The company also takes the security of customer data seriously, which is a meaningful positive.
cons:
Upper management can sometimes make employees feel more like numbers than individuals. There has also been a noticeable shift toward reducing costs and relying more heavily on lower paid engineering roles supported by AI. While AI can be an effective tool, this change has left some experienced engineers feeling undervalued and uncertain about their future. At the same time, engineering support has become more limited, and workloads are often difficult to manage.

Case volumes have increased significantly. Engineers were initially told to expect approximately 12 to 15 cases, but toward the end, some workloads approached 40 cases per engineer. Although employees are permitted to take vacation, there may not be enough team coverage to manage their cases in their absence, which can result in a substantial backlog upon their return. Engineers are generally expected to adapt to these circumstances, even when that means working late to keep up.

There are efforts to help balance workloads, but those efforts are limited when other engineers are already at capacity. As a result, customer resolutions can be delayed. With so many cases and limited time, engineers must prioritize, which often means responding first to the most urgent or persistent requests. Customers who ask for fewer updates may unintentionally receive less attention, not because their concerns are less important, but because engineers are managing more work than they can reasonably complete.

There is also a strong expectation that engineers call customers, even when those customers have indicated that they prefer email. Email can be an efficient and effective way to resolve certain cases, particularly for customers who do not have time for a call. However, there appears to be greater emphasis on phone interactions because they are more likely to generate survey responses.

Employee feedback does not always seem to result in meaningful changes. For example, an employee survey was distributed shortly before employees were informed that there would be no bonuses or merit increases that year. The timing made it feel as though the survey results may have been affected by information employees had not yet received. While employees are encouraged to share their opinions, there can be a perception that the organization is more interested in collecting feedback than in addressing the concerns behind it.

The company now places a strong emphasis on AI, and some employees feel that the culture many people valued at Microsoft has changed significantly. Recognition and rewards have become less common, and managers may have limited influence over decisions affecting their engineers as the organization focuses increasingly on reducing costs. Customer survey results also appear to carry significant weight, sometimes even when obtaining a survey response requires more effort than resolving the original case.

Staffing levels have often felt insufficient, and the continued push to use AI may further reduce headcount, even though AI is not always accurate. AI can be a valuable tool for engineers, but it should complement human expertise rather than replace or diminish the value of experienced engineers.

I believe many of these challenges extend beyond direct management, and that managers may also feel constrained by broader organizational decisions. It would be encouraging to see Microsoft place greater emphasis on employee well being and mental health through meaningful changes, rather than relying solely on the availability of support services.

Providing engineers with clearer expectations, manageable workloads, adequate staffing, and the resources needed to succeed could help reduce stress and improve overall performance. Greater transparency about the company’s direction and potential changes would also help employees feel more informed and secure about the future.

summary: Politics and fear overshadow talented colleagues at Netflix
pros: High performing colleagues, interesting content, good corporae structure, benefits and support.
cons:
Lack of diversity.

Netflix's culture no longer resembles the "dream team" it built its reputation on.

Performance alone is no longer enough. Managing upwards and protecting the right relationships seem to matter more than consistently delivering great work. Exceptional individual contributors become poor people managers, yet continue to progress without meaningful accountability.

There are many talented, hardworking people at Netflix, but they're increasingly overshadowed by politics, self-promotion, and a culture of fear. People are often reluctant to speak openly or even associate with former colleagues because leadership can change its view of you overnight.

The company is quick to move on individual contributors but appears far less willing to question ineffective leadership, even when teams experience repeated turnover.

Netflix is still full of brilliant people, but the culture that once made it exceptional has, been lost.

Comp is good when you start but you can spend 3-4 years without an increase and there are no bonuses. You're better off working in a lower paid, psychologically safe entertainment company for the long term. If any exist.
advice:
The diversity of thought that once made Netflix exceptional feels diminished, and that's a real loss.

Take a hard look at middle management. Too many ineffective managers become bottlenecks, failing upwards, while talented, experienced people leave. Leadership should be held as accountable for team performance and retention as individual contributors are for theirs.

The market for exceptional talent is more competitive than ever, particularly with AI companies actively hiring. Losing great people because of poor management is an avoidable mistake.

Finally, make sure decisions are driven by evidence and creative excellence rather than internal politics or popularity. When culture shifts in that direction, audiences eventually notice. In my view, the quality and consistency of the content are already beginning to reflect it.

summary: Culture has shifted from trust to constant monitoring
pros:
Used to be great,
No Pros currently
cons:
15 Years In — The Culture Has Become Exhausting

After 15 years with Citi, I never thought I would describe the workplace this way, but the level of monitoring and pressure has become overwhelming.

Salaried employees are being tracked by computer/VDI activity, office attendance, and how long they remain onsite. We are required to report to the office three days a week, and employees feel they have to stay a minimum number of hours to avoid being flagged or questioned. When salaried professionals with years of proven performance feel anxious about stepping away for a doctor’s appointment or taking care of their children because they are worried about how their activity will look, something is seriously wrong with the culture.

Many Tampa-area employees commute an hour or more each way, only to sit at a computer doing work that can largely be performed remotely. Add commuting costs, expensive onsite food, and the rising cost of living in Tampa Bay while salaries have not kept pace, and employees are understandably frustrated.

This also comes after the COVID era, when employees faced vaccination requirements tied to continued employment. Now, years later, many of us feel we have moved from one form of control to another—attendance tracking, VDI hours, onsite time, and constant scrutiny.

After 15 years, I should feel trusted based on my performance and experience—not monitored like a timecard. Salaried professionals should be evaluated by the quality of their work, results, accountability, and contribution, not whether a computer shows them logged in for a certain number of hours.

The company talks about flexibility, employee well-being, and work-life balance, but the day-to-day experience can feel very different. People with families are stressed. Long-term employees feel mistrusted. Morale suffers when experienced professionals feel watched instead of valued.

Citi needs to remember that employees are people, not activity metrics. Trust your people, measure their results, compensate them appropriately for today’s cost of living, and give them enough flexibility to have a life outside of work.

summary: PwC Company Review
pros:
1. Strong Learning Culture — The company invests heavily in employee development with quarterly training budgets, conference attendance, and mentorship programs. You'll grow your skills fast.

2. Competitive Compensation & Benefits — Solid salary, comprehensive health insurance, 401(k) matching, unlimited PTO, and remote work flexibility. Financial security is solid.

3. Cutting-Edge Tech Stack — Work with modern technologies (TypeScript, React, AWS, Kubernetes). Your resume stays relevant and you build marketable skills.

4. Collaborative Team Environment — Small, tight-knit engineering team with open communication. Flat hierarchy means your ideas get heard and implemented.

5. Clear Growth Path
cons:
1. High Pressure & Fast Pace — Startup mentality means tight deadlines, frequent pivots, and "move fast and break things" culture. Burnout is real, especially during product launches.

2. Inconsistent Work-Life Balance — While remote-friendly, the expectation is often to be "always on." Weekend Slack messages and late-night emergency fixes are common.

3. Limited Resources & Budget — As a growing company, resources are stretched. You'll often do more with less — no fancy tools, older hardware, hiring lags behind workload.

4. Unclear Product Direction — Leadership frequently changes strategy based on market feedback. Projects get deprioritized or scrapped midway, leading to frustration and wasted effort.

5. Early-Stage Compensation Concerns — While salary is decent, equity is uncertain. If the company doesn't succeed, that stock option package becomes worthless. Financial risk.

summary: Identical work, unequal pay, zero transparency
pros: Sadly nothing positive to note, even though I started out genuinely excited about the role.
cons: I'm leaving this review because of unfair pay structures and poor communication from management. People doing identical work in the same role are paid very differently, with no discernible justification for where anyone lands and no difference in experience or responsibility to explain the gap. How pay is decided was never explained, discussing it is effectively off-limits, and management becomes evasive whenever the topic comes up. At the same time, expectations and performance pressure are high in a way that feels disconnected from what people are actually paid. Communication was also weak from the very start of the process, with vague expectations and little transparency about compensation. Overall, it's an environment where equal work is very unequally rewarded, exactly the kind of situation that makes real pay transparency more necessary than ever.
advice: Don't hide behind contract structures to justify paying people very differently for identical work. Build a clear pay framework, make it transparent, and communicate honestly.

summary: Worst company experience with poor leadership and culture
pros: Unfortunately, I cannot identify any meaningful pros from my experience at EY. The experience did, however, give me clarity about the type of company culture and leadership environment I do not want to work in again.
cons:
Hands down the worst company I have ever worked for in my professional career.

My experience at EY was characterized by poor leadership, lack of transparency, inconsistent communication, and an overall culture that felt impersonal and unsupportive. There was a significant disconnect between the values the organization promotes publicly and what I experienced as an employee.

Expectations and priorities were not always communicated clearly, yet employees were still expected to deliver at an extremely high level. Leadership and management practices often created unnecessary stress rather than providing employees with the direction, support, and resources needed to succeed.

The size and reputation of EY may look impressive from the outside, but a prestigious name does not automatically translate into a positive employee experience. I have worked for several large, complex organizations throughout my career, and my experience at EY was by far the most disappointing.

I left with a much greater appreciation for organizations that value transparency, communication, accountability, and treating experienced professionals with respect.
advice:
Listen to your employees—especially experienced professionals who were hired because of the expertise they bring to the organization. Leadership should focus less on corporate messaging and more on whether the employee experience actually reflects the values EY claims to promote.

Better communication, clearer expectations, stronger accountability for managers, and more genuine investment in employees would go a long way. A company’s reputation should not be used as a substitute for good leadership and a healthy workplace culture.

summary: Disappointing experience - limited HR support, impersonal exit process
pros: Decent exposure to enterprise-scale BI projects and tools like Power BI and Microsoft Fabric, particularly useful for those early in their career.
cons:
There were difficulties even before my start date. I was hired against a Bangalore posting but was based in Pune, and requests for clarification prior to joining went unanswered. Having already resigned from my previous role by that point, I proceeded with the relocation without further clarity.

HR was difficult to reach throughout my tenure, with limited proactive communication or support.

There was no bench support between projects. Rather than being staffed directly, I went through repeated rounds of project interviews with little continuity or clear ownership of staffing decisions from management.

Work-life balance was a significant concern. Leave requests were frequently denied, and weekend work was expected without additional compensation.

The exit process was the most disappointing part. I was told that resigning would leave "no record" of it, which did not prove accurate. My EPF Form-19 settlement has also been pending for over a month; the EPFO helpline, regional office emails/calls, and an in-person visit have not led to a resolution despite multiple grievances filed.

Overall, I found the support structure lacking at every stage — hiring, staffing, and offboarding.
advice: Improve HR responsiveness starting from the hiring stage. Build a more consistent project-staffing process so employees aren't repeatedly re-interviewing without ownership. Reconsider leave policies and weekend work expectations. Ensure communication around resignation and exit procedures is accurate. Streamline the offboarding process so departing employees can access their settlements without extended delays.

summary: Toxic "No-Growth" Growth Culture & Deceptive Exit Communications
pros: Strong global brand name on your resume, decent infrastructure, and an unpredictable corporate environment.
cons: The "No-Growth" Growth Culture: Management heavily promotes a narrative of career progression and continuous upskilling, but the internal reality is structural stagnation. You are constantly handed "stretch assignments" to handle higher-level responsibilities under the guise of "proving your readiness for a promotion." However, the goalposts are always moving. When review season arrives, promotions are stalled due to sudden budget cuts or subjective metrics, leaving you doing senior-level work on a junior salary with a stagnant tech stack.Deceptive and Vague Exit Process: Transparency is entirely lacking when you decide to leave. If you request an early release and managers approve it via email using terms like "shortfall days will be adjusted against your financial settlement," beware. They use the ambiguous word "adjusted" as a legal loophole to aggressively claw back and deduct your gross salary for those unserved days from your earned wages. Instead of clearly breaking down the financial penalty or offering a transparent waiver process up front, they hide behind vague wording to process heavy deductions in your final Full & Final (F&F) statement.
advice:
Stop using marketing buzzwords to trick ambitious talent into dead-end operational roles with no actual career trajectory. Furthermore, mandate that HR and managers explicitly specify exact monetary recovery terms in writing using clear words like "deducted" rather than misleading employees with ambiguous terms like "adjusted."
Give good growth opportunities and increment to talented employees rather than paying more to external hires all the time.

summary: Strong benefits and flexibility but management issues persist
pros: Oracle offers strong benefits, generous PTO, remote work flexibility, and opportunities to work with talented colleagues and complex customers.  I have had meaningful opportunities to develop people, create new processes and tools, solve challenging customer problems, and grow across multiple roles. There are many employees who care about their customers and one another.
cons:
The employee experience can depend almost entirely on the manager and organization you happen to report into.  Priorities and expectations frequently shift as leadership changes direction, sometimes without adequate communication or consideration for the teams responsible for carrying out those decisions. 

Across multiple leadership structures, I experienced a lack of psychological safety. Questions, misunderstandings, or perceived mistakes could quickly become tense and accusatory rather than being handled through calm fact-finding and collaborative problem solving.  In some cases, conclusions were made before all facts were understood.  Even when the original concern proved unfounded.  The stress and damaged caused by the escalation remained.  

Employees are expected to remain adaptable, support their teams, and absorb org changes, but that same support is not always returned to employees.  Strong performance and a long record of positive results do not necessarily protect one from micromanagement, shifting standards, or communication that gradually undermines their confidence. 

There also appears to be major tension between organizations and levels of leadership, with decisions sometimes driven by competing internal priorities rather than what is best for employees and customers.  Over time this creates, fear, burnout, and unnecessary anxiety among otherwise capable and committed employees.
advice:
Invest in leadership accountability and require managers to demonstrate emotional intelligence, not just operations results. Encourage leaders to verify facts before assigning blame, address concerns private and respectfully, and treat mistakes and misunderstandings as opportunities for problem solving rather than personal failure. 

Create meaningful way for employees to report harmful management patterns without fearing retaliation.  Pay attention when successful long tenured employees begin struggling under a particular leadership structure. Psychological safety, consistent expectations, and respectful communication should be measured as seriously as revenue and performance metrics.

pros: They have a reputation for getting work, so they do hire.
cons:
Bad work life balance. I'd worked with IPC before the pandemic. I told myself I wouldn't be back after my stint with them pre-pandemic, but they were the only place hiring in 2024 so I had to come back. Unfortunately, the company's attitude towards their freelancers has declined since then. IPC is known for their content and they do produce great tv shows, but they do it at the expense of their employees. Their first big show was Emmy-nominated and critically beloved, but it came at the expense of the staff on the show. The host of the show was particularly cruel to the staff and for a long time, IPC turned a blind eye to her treatment of staff because the show was so big.

I've come back now and that show is now gone. The outright cruelty isn't there, but the disregard for the staff is still present. Unfortunately, the industry seems to be shifting towards a pattern of creating high content with low budgets. IPC has gladly embraced that and is inking deals with low budgets while still expecting crew to pick up the slack. Productions have very little budget and reduced support on set while still expected to delivery high-quality content. Post works extremely long hours to try to pick up the slack and IPC is more than happy that people work from home now so they can "keep working". Requests for more help are ignored until the problems are too big and teams are scrambling to catch up.

If you can hang with this, they do hire and seem to re-hire people they like working with. Or, most accurately, re-hire people they know will work their crazy schedules. If you're planning on taking a job with them, be clear about your availability and the schedule they're requesting.
advice: Care about your people. Reduce your overhead if you need to rather than reducing the help needed on your projects. CARE ABOUT YOUR PEOPLE.

summary: Layoff Culture is King
pros:
I would give the rest of my career to Cisco if I was given the opportunity. This is by far the best culture, team, and company I have worked for in my multi decade career. 

Pros: 
- One Cisco, Many Careers is true -- this organization is built for entrepreneurial spirits, and in the right environments, one can create their own career aligned with their passions and talents. 
- Data readiness. Cisco is working on improving their data story and if they continue on this path will improve operations, and thus culture. I see data readiness, and subsequent actioning of the data, as a the saving grace for Cisco's operations (improving decision velocity, reducing waste, and aligning our focus to priority). 
- Some of the best leaders and colleagues you will ever work with. When supported well, teams at Cisco operate from a place of abundance, where the work is a shared responsibility. We are team together and we support and skill each other up in the process. Teamwork at Cisco has been the most productive out of any place I've worked.
cons:
Layoff culture dominates all others. You cannot build a meaningful feedback culture, growth mindset, or AI-ready workforce when the psychological contract between employee and employer is routinely (and predictably) disrupted.

In more than six years at Cisco, I have experienced repeated layoffs, reorganizations, and transformations (every. single. quarter). Each one carries a recovery cost that rarely appears on a restructuring spreadsheet. Teams have to rebuild trust, redistribute work, onboard new colleagues, redefine roles, and relearn how decisions get made. Too often, that recovery is still underway when the next organizational change begins.

I have personally supported multiple transformations that should have been relatively straightforward but never fully landed—not necessarily because the strategy was wrong, but because the organization repeatedly lost the focus, continuity, and sustained effort that meaningful change requires, as the result of constant restructuring. 

The consequence and data for leaders to explore centers on change fatigue. 

Teams spend enormous energy regrounding: rebuilding relationships, clarifying responsibilities, establishing new ways of working, and trying to create psychological safety again. That is capacity no longer being spent on priorities like AI transformation, skills development, customer outcomes, or executing the strategy employees were previously asked to rally behind.

I encourage leaders to look at their history -- how many times have we deprioritized an intiative (like a PLP) so that we could ground a land a newly formed team with something like Instinctive Drives and an offsite? You are forming the beginnings of a great business school lesson of how NOT to sustain a positive culture. 

Personally, I love Cisco more than any company I have ever worked for and I will not go quietly. That said, I am not going quietly (I am typing it out) and sharing that my security requires action. I am a top performing leader, but even I am devoting five hours of my working week to look for more secure employment, and when that offer comes I won't think twice. Security matters more than salary for this employee. 

You cannot continuously disrupt the organization and simultaneously expect employees to transform it -- or stick around.
advice:
1) Pay attention to the canaries. Our employee voice scores are showing you the issues to address. 
2) ELT needs upskilling in radical (not reckless) transparency. Some leaders yell and say, "adopt AI or get runover." Others lead people by explaining how employees fit into the situation you are asking them to enter.... I am still learning who was impacted from the last LR (not great comms and terrible for trust/culture -- imagine being surprised that the 30 year employee, seemingly top performer, and person who hired me was let go when you were reaching out to ask them an important question about the work they owned). 
3) Get out of your way. We have a proven way of operating through layoffs -- it is not up for debate -- Cisco is a layoff culture. What innovation can come from deeper questions rooted in innovation? I've noticed we are quick with the solution but rarely fully diagnose the problem (e.g., "everyone use AI." vs. "I've noticed we have an opportunity in project governance and scope -- how can AI help keep us on track?"

Finally, I am getting a lot of reminders of Kodak, and I think that is the path Cisco might be headed down and it scares me. In short, Kodak failed but it wasn't their inability to embrace new technology (they invented the digital camera in 1975). Similarities from Kodak that I am seeing at Cisco: 
1) Promote transformation but neglect the cost (time) of behavior change required to realize it. 
2) Struggle to activate meaningfully with the technology. When technology serves the sole purpose of being novel, not to solve a business issue, it distracts and steals from the bottom line. Tech cannot replace people and will not alone solve our business issues (so we buckle up for another layoff). 
3) Transformation is ambiguous/unclear. We talk about transformation but revert to old habits and routine behaviors that sustain a status quo. Specifically, what is the BUSINESS metric that will tell us we are successful with AI (not adoption, how are we improving our business)?
4) Lost institutional knowledge and continuity as a result of continuous restructuring. A pattern of routine layoffs began in 1982 and continued until the demise of Kodak in 2013, with one former Kodak leader sharing: "Donwsizing often fails to deliver what leaders expect. Anticipated benefits, such as improved productivity, profitability, entrepreneurship, and smother communication frequently failed to materialize after downsizing." 

Perhaps this is because they were too busy reforming their team and working on their Instinctive Drives.... 

Finally, would I put this much effort into this review if I didn't love Cisco? I want to save Cisco from itself.

summary: Real scale, strong engineers, and genuine ownership - tempered by constant reorganizations.
pros:
The scale of the problems is real and hard to find elsewhere. Strong engineers, and real autonomy. Infrastructure and architecture decisions access. 

Genuine investment in people development.

Global collaboration across multiple countries is normal and works well in practice, not just on paper. Recognition programs are meaningful. 

Work flexibility (even when stated full time on site).
cons:
Repeated reorganizations make long-term planning difficult and cost good people. The engineering knowledge lost in each cycle is considerably larger than the headcount number suggests, and much of the following year goes on rebuilding it.

Strategic direction has narrowed substantially over the years. Commercially defensible, but it means the technical breadth of the work is smaller than it once was, and that is a real factor for engineers who joined for the harder problems.

Integrating teams from acquisitions brings inconsistent engineering practices.

Decisin-making is slow at scale and priorities shift between planning cycles.
advice:
Protect engineering continuity through reorganisations. The institutional knowledge lost each
cycle is worth more than the headcount saved, and it does not show up on the spreadsheet that
justified the change.

When two groups merge, choose one engineering methodology deliberately and resource the migration properly. Letting both run in parallel indefinitely is the most expensive option available and it is usually the one taken by default.

Give seniors visibility of direction beyond the current quarter. We are asked to plan development on a horizon we are not allowed to see, and engineers can tell when their management is improvising.

summary: 27 Years of Service — A Difficult Ending
pros: Good pay and benefits, strong union wages in represented positions, opportunities to learn valuable technical and customer-service skills, and the chance to build lasting relationships with coworkers and customers. Over many years, I worked alongside some truly great people and leaders who took pride in their work and supported their teams.
cons:
After more than 27 years with Verizon, one of the biggest disappointments was seeing how much an employee’s experience could depend on the management team they worked under.

In my experience, poor leadership, inconsistent treatment, and a culture where employees could feel afraid to challenge management created an unnecessarily stressful work environment. Employees should be able to raise legitimate concerns or disagree with management without feeling that doing so could put a target on their back.

There also seemed to be a disconnect between the values promoted at the corporate level and what employees could experience at the local management level. Accountability needs to work both ways. Employees are expected to follow policies and meet high standards, but managers should be held to equally high standards regarding professionalism, fairness, communication, and how they treat their employees.

After investing decades of my career in the company, I learned an important lesson: a great company name cannot compensate for poor leadership at the local level.

Verizon has many talented and hardworking employees. They deserve leaders who listen to them, respect them, develop them, and understand that leadership is about earning trust—not simply having authority.
advice: Listen to your employees, especially those who have dedicated many years to the company. Hold managers accountable, apply policies consistently, and create an environment where employees can raise concerns without fear of being labeled as difficult. Leadership should be about earning trust, developing people, and treating everyone with fairness and respect. A strong company starts with leaders who are willing to listen and hold themselves to the same standards they expect from their employees.

summary: A Remarkable Company Buried Under Years of Acquisitions, Debt and Layoffs
pros: AT&T has extraordinary history, scale and institutional knowledge. I worked with many genuinely talented people during my 7½ years there and had opportunities to work on large, complex initiatives that affected substantial parts of the business. I learned a tremendous amount, did work I remain proud of, and received recognition for some of it. There are people at AT&T with decades of expertise who understand an extraordinarily complicated business in ways that would be difficult to replace.
cons:
Years of acquisitions, reorganizations, cost cutting, and repeated layoffs created an environment in which instability eventually became normal.

I joined AT&T in 2016 and spent 7½ years there. During that time, successive rounds of restructuring steadily reduced teams and institutional knowledge. When positions disappeared, the work frequently did not disappear with them. Remaining employees absorbed additional responsibilities, organizational boundaries shifted, and people spent significant energy trying to determine who still owned what.

That eventually creates its own inefficiency. A company can remove positions faster than it removes complexity. Work that should be straightforward can become unnecessarily difficult when responsibilities are fragmented across organizations, legacy processes, and multiple stakeholders. Repeated restructuring may reduce headcount on paper while simultaneously making the remaining work harder to execute.

The acquisition strategy also had enormous consequences. AT&T spent years pursuing businesses such as DirecTV and Time Warner, then later unwound significant portions of that strategy. Employees obviously had no control over decisions made at that level, but they repeatedly experienced the consequences through reorganizations, shifting priorities, cost reductions, and layoffs.

The most damaging part was the persistent uncertainty. After enough rounds of layoffs, employees inevitably begin wondering whether they will be next. That affects morale, willingness to take risks, long-term planning, and eventually retention. People with valuable institutional knowledge leave voluntarily, others are eliminated, and the remaining organization becomes increasingly dependent on fewer people who understand how everything actually works.

The tone from the top did not always help. During this period, CEO John Stankey made remarks in employee forums that many employees understood as dismissive of older, long-tenured workers, including comments about AT&T not needing people who knew how to use an “abacus” and that if you knew what a “dial tone” was, it was time to go. Whether those remarks were intended as shorthand for modernization or not, they landed badly in an organization already eliminating large numbers of experienced employees.

That is a particularly unfortunate message for a company whose competitive advantage was built over generations by people who understood the network, the technology, the customers, and the extraordinarily complicated machinery behind the business. Modernization is necessary. Treating experience as synonymous with obsolescence is not.

AT&T also developed a culture in which repeated layoffs became so routine that employees learned to live with the possibility of being eliminated almost continuously. That kind of environment drains attention and trust. People cannot be expected to simultaneously worry about whether their organization will exist next quarter and devote themselves fully to building something for the long term.

My own position was ultimately eliminated after 7½ years. By then, I had survived multiple restructurings and watched numerous talented colleagues leave before me.

AT&T still has extraordinary assets: its network, brand, technical expertise, history, and people. But repeated restructuring has a cost that does not always appear immediately on a balance sheet. Institutional knowledge, employee trust, and organizational capability take years to build and can disappear remarkably quickly.
advice:
AT&T is one of the most historically important American companies. This is American Telephone and Telegraph. Few corporations have a legacy of innovation, engineering and technical achievement comparable to it.

Treat that institutional knowledge as an asset.

Cost reduction may sometimes be necessary, but continually reducing headcount while expecting the remaining organization to absorb the same complexity eventually produces diminishing returns. Before eliminating positions, examine whether the work, processes and organizational complexity associated with those positions are actually being eliminated as well.

AT&T would also benefit from greater organizational stability. Employees cannot continuously operate as though another restructuring may be around the corner and simultaneously be expected to think creatively, take risks and build for the long term.

Most importantly, recognize the cumulative cost of losing experienced employees. Some people at AT&T have spent years learning systems, products, organizations and processes that are extraordinarily difficult for outsiders to understand quickly. Once enough of that knowledge walks out the door, rebuilding it is considerably harder than removing it was.

AT&T does not lack talent. It does not lack history, resources or capability. What it has lacked at times is stability and a sufficiently long-term view of its own workforce.

A company can restructure itself into greater efficiency.

It can also restructure itself into amnesia.

summary: Strong benefits, but customer focus needs improvement
pros: AT&T has been a rewarding company to work for, offering employees valuable benefits and resources that contribute to a positive overall experience. Perks such as discounted service and generous paid time off are especially appreciated and stand out compared with those offered by many other companies. These benefits demonstrate an investment in employees and provide meaningful support for both their professional and personal lives. While there are always opportunities for continued growth and improvement, AT&T offers many advantages that make it a good place to build a career.
cons: I believe AT&T would benefit from renewing its commitment to placing customers at the center of its decisions rather than prioritizing financial outcomes above the customer experience. Although we are consistently told that the customer is the primary focus, that message does not always appear to be reflected in the company’s actions or decisions. During my tenure with AT&T, I have observed what seems to be a gradual decline in this customer-first approach.
advice:
Please remain open to listening to employees and thoughtfully considering their ideas and feedback. The workplace is continually evolving, and an approach that works well today may need to be adjusted in the months or years ahead. Employees often bring valuable perspectives based on their day-to-day experiences, and giving them a voice can help the organization grow stronger.

It is also important for leaders to consistently treat employees with professionalism, trust, and respect. Whenever possible, employees should be given the autonomy to perform their responsibilities, demonstrate their capabilities, and prove their value without excessive oversight. Unless performance concerns indicate that closer guidance is necessary, empowering employees to take ownership of their work can build confidence, strengthen morale, and support better results.

My hope is that management will continue creating an environment where employees feel heard, respected, trusted, and motivated to do their best work.

summary: Nearly 20 Years in Sales, and Nothing Prepared Me for This
pros: The company has a decent benefits package.
cons:
After nearly 20 years in B2B and enterprise sales, this was, without question, the worst employment experience of my career.

I accepted what was advertised as an outside sales position. Instead, I felt like I had accepted a job in an inside sales call center.

Every day revolved around Microsoft Teams. I was added to what felt like 50 different Teams chats for every imaginable purpose. There were chats for announcements, activity tracking, territories, blitz calls, the “Zero Club,” training, management, and countless others. From the moment you logged in until the end of the day, it was nonstop. People were expected to say “good morning,” constantly respond to chats, post updates, and keep up with an endless stream of notifications. I spent more time staring at Teams than I did talking to customers. It felt like being chained to a computer instead of working in outside sales.

Then there was Gong.

I fundamentally disagree with AI being used to coach experienced sales professionals. In my opinion, AI has no business replacing real leadership and real coaching. Instead of feeling supported, I felt like I was under constant surveillance. Customer calls, internal conversations, coaching sessions - it felt like nearly everything was recorded, analyzed, and critiqued. The entire culture reminded me of George Orwell’s 1984. I honestly felt like I couldn’t even think my own thoughts without feeling like someone was watching. It was mentally exhausting.

The micromanagement was unlike anything I’ve experienced in nearly two decades of professional sales.

The daily blitz calls were absurd. Imagine trying to prospect while connected to a Microsoft Teams meeting with dozens of other sales representatives talking in the background. Managers would have people make cold calls in front of everyone while the rest of the group listened. It wasn’t motivating. It wasn’t coaching. It was distracting, uncomfortable, and humiliating.

If you didn’t produce sales almost immediately, you were publicly placed into something called the “Zero Club.” Publicly labeling new hires who haven’t yet closed business isn’t leadership. It’s demeaning and demoralizing.

Here’s the irony:  I wanted to prospect, I wanted to knock on doors, I wanted to meet customers face to face. That’s what outside sales is supposed to be.

Instead, I was told I had to submit a list of businesses I planned to visit and have it approved before I could even leave the office to do the job I was hired to do. In nearly 20 years of sales, I have never experienced anything like that.

Management was my biggest disappointment.

Communication was poor. One on one meetings were frequently canceled, rescheduled, or started late. Calendars seemed to mean very little, and there was little respect for other people’s time.

During my first week, and repeatedly throughout my time there, my manager told me, “Book meetings and I’ll help you close them. I’ll be there.” I believed him. Over the next three months, I invited him to every customer meeting I scheduled.

He didn’t attend a single one. Not one.

There were no messages beforehand, no explanation afterward, and no follow up. I kept doing exactly what I was told to do, and the support I was promised never materialized.

If you’re going to tell a new sales representative you’ll be there to help close business, then show up. If you can’t, communicate. Don’t repeatedly make promises you have no intention of keeping.

Despite bringing nearly 20 years of successful B2B and enterprise sales experience to the table, I was treated as though I had never sold before. Instead of trusting experienced professionals, the culture seemed built around monitoring activity rather than producing results.

The office itself deserves its own section because I’ve never seen anything like it in my professional life.

From the first day I walked into that building, I wanted out. It looked less like the office of one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world and more like the set of a zombie apocalypse movie. Cubicles sat abandoned and overflowing with what looked like decades-old equipment, trash, and junk. The entire place felt neglected, dirty, and forgotten.

What disturbed me most were the sanitation conditions. I personally observed rodent droppings on multiple floors of the building. There were cockroaches, dead insects, and rodent droppings inside a refrigerator employees were expected to use. The bathrooms were DISGUSTING...they were not cleaned once during my short time there, and probably not for years before that.  The building had a constant unpleasant odor, and I routinely left with headaches. It was, without exaggeration, the FILTHIEST, MOST DISGUST AND ABHORRENT workplace I have ever seen.

If a restaurant had been maintained the way this office was (wasn't), it would have been shut down by the health department. I couldn’t believe this was the workplace of a 180 BILLION DOLLAR COMPANY.

The conditions became serious enough that OSHA conducted an inspection while I was employed there. Even after that, I was left wondering why employees were expected to work in an environment like this.

I’ve worked in office buildings, customer sites, data centers, warehouses, and construction environments throughout my career. None of them came close to the condition of this office.

Even leaving the company was a disaster.

I gave notice professionally. Instead of a normal offboarding process, my employment simply ended. There was no exit interview, no explanation of the separation process, and no communication about final pay information, benefits, or how to access basic employment records. Five business days later, I had to contact HR myself just to determine what had happened and how to obtain the information I needed.

Looking back, I spent more time sitting in Teams meetings, responding to chats, tracking activity, and being monitored than I did actually selling.

That’s backwards.

If you’re an experienced sales professional looking for autonomy, trust, and the opportunity to build customer relationships, my experience was the complete opposite.

This company hired me for outside sales, but what I actually experienced felt like working in a heavily monitored virtual call center inside one of the most neglected office buildings I’ve ever stepped foot in.

Do yourself a favor and look for employment elsewhere.
advice:
Start trusting your people.

If you hire experienced sales professionals, let them sell. Stop burying them in Microsoft Teams, endless chat groups, unnecessary meetings, activity reports, surveillance, and bureaucracy that take them away from customers.

Technology should support employees, not make them feel like they’re being watched every minute of the day. Real coaching comes from experienced leaders who show up, keep their promises, and develop their people - not from AI analyzing every conversation.

Respect employees’ calendars. Respect their experience. If you tell a new hire you’ll support them in customer meetings, show up. If you promise coaching, provide it. If you expect professionalism from your employees, demonstrate it yourselves.

Most importantly, take pride in your workplace. No employee should have to work in an office plagued by sanitation issues, rodents, insects, and conditions serious enough to warrant an OSHA inspection.

Great sales organizations don’t succeed by treating experienced professionals like they’re under constant surveillance. They succeed by hiring good people, trusting them, supporting them, and giving them the freedom to build customer relationships and produce results.

The work is challenging and exposes you to a wide range of technologies, including HFC, fiber, network maintenance, emergency restoration, and infrastructure projects. cons: Frequent organizational changes, increasing workload, and uncertainty about the company's long-term direction have hurt morale. Career advancement can feel inconsistent, and experienced employees may not always feel their technical expertise is recognized or utilized effectively. Communication between leadership and field teams could be stronger.
advice:
Invest in retaining experienced employees by recognizing technical expertise, creating clear advancement paths, and improving communication between leadership and field operations. Continue developing future talent while ensuring promotions and compensation are based on demonstrated skills, performance, leadership, and the ability to solve complex problems.

One area that deserves immediate attention is the current pay progression. Under the existing structure, a new Network Technician can surpass the pay of a technician with 10 years of experience in as little as five years. That sends the wrong message to long-term employees who have invested years developing specialized skills and institutional knowledge. A compensation structure that better rewards experience, expertise, and long-term contributions would improve retention and help preserve the technical knowledge that keeps the network running.

summary: Not enough pixie dust to make this tolerable
pros: The only real benefit is having the Disney brand name on your resume. Aside from the standard corporate perks or employee discounts, there is very little to praise about the day-to-day reality of working here
cons:
Toxic Environment: The culture is bogged down by rampant office politics and blatant misogyny that goes completely unchecked.

Stifled Innovation: There is zero interest in original thinking. Leadership consistently presents "rinse and repeat" ideas and expects you to fall in line.

Outdated Operations: The department is completely anchored to archaic processes with absolutely no appetite for modernization or efficiency.

Lazy Cost Management: Instead of doing the work to negotiate better terms, the company just inflates prices for the consumer.
advice:
This was, without a doubt, the worst job I have ever had. If you are expecting a forward-thinking, collaborative, or magical workplace, you will be incredibly disappointed. The culture is rife with heavy-handed politics, and at its core, there is an underlying current of misogyny that makes it a genuinely toxic place to work.

From a business and operational standpoint, it is a frustrating black hole. Leadership has no interest in breaking out of archaic processes. Every presentation is just a "rinse and repeat" of the same recycled ideas. Worse, for a company with this much global leverage, there is a shocking lack of understanding of how to actually use our purchasing power. Instead of planning effectively and negotiating better costing with vendors, the default strategy is always the easiest one: just pass the increased costs directly onto the consumer. It is lazy business management and incredibly demoralizing to execute.  For a company that continues to say they care about their guests, these guests would be appealed at the way the company callously continues to increase retails purely bc they believe their "fan it alls" will shell out the cash.  I kid you not, I'd sit in meetings where planning, location strategy, brand and merchandising would chant "money, money, money" or send dollar sign emojis in the chat in order to express excitement for a new product. 

Advice to Management
Take a hard look at the toxic, misogynistic culture you are fostering before you lose more talent. Stop leaning on the brand name as an excuse for poor management. Finally, learn how to leverage your supply chain and purchasing power to negotiate costs, rather than treating the consumer’s wallet as your only strategy for margin growth.  Look at all the redundant and inefficient decision making practices and start with leadership if you need to cut more roles, which you will in the next few months...its clear cast members are expendable given their regular practice of layoffs, so start with the top.

cons:

- Compared to Starwood, many systems are outdated and inefficient.  
- No real moral support: if the owner wants you out, the company will not defend you, even when you are in the right.  
- They show little concern for the owner's asset; the primary focus is on management fees and incentives.  
- Local talent is often overlooked in favor of expatriates from Europe, the US, etc., even when local expertise already exists or only needs development.  
- They do not teach the "real stuff" (e.g., finance); that knowledge is reserved for expatriates. Local employees are treated as labor to execute on the floor, not as people to develop and grow.
advice: Live the "People First" value genuinely. Invest in local talent development, modernize systems, and support your associates when they are right, rather than prioritizing fees and expatriate placements.

summary: Toxic Mold and even more Toxic Manager response almost lead to employee's death
pros: I mean, they hire pretty much anyone, people who are homeless, people with substance abuse issues, people who served time in jail...
cons:
I should have asked the coworker if he/she wanted help getting legal support, but I didn’t. It’s one of the biggest regrets I have.

What happened to this person sickened me and made me want to quit my job immediately. 

Years ago there was a coworker who wanted to eventually get a managerial promotion. 

This coworker got very sick with mold in the air vents and had to be hospitalized multiple times. The Head of Maintenance and the Operations/General Manager both knew what type of mold was in the air vents as the coworker who got sick saw them attempting to clean, and eventually carrying out the vents to be replaced (right above the front desk). However, neither of them disclosed the type of mold the coworker was sick with so he/she could not get proper treatment and had to stay in the hospital longer than he/she would have if they told the hospital the type of mold. 

I can understand if the company head honchos wanted to cover up the negligence, and the manager and Maintenance Head both wanted to prevent backlash from their bosses, but it’s such a despicable lack of empathy and human decency. If ever there was a time to grow a spine and defy the company’s upper upper management, it would have been during this time of life or death. The coworker almost died but didn’t want to sue for fear of losing more than 25 years of loyal work for Marriott. Here’s the kicker: It’s been years since that incident and the coworker isn’t a manager. All those years of loyalty for nothing. Less than nothing, since the coworker was hurt. Marriott does not and never will reward employee loyalty or service.

Also an unrelated note, one of those branch managers was in the employee break room one day, complaining about his/her salary. If you’re lucky enough to be a branch manager, don’t complain to the lowest of the low housekeeping employees that you don’t feel you’re paid enough. It’s laughable. Marriott employees get about $1 raise per year. No performance review, no bonuses, no chance for anything more. Of course, it’s probably different if you’re a manager.

Speaking of managers, the managers do like to abuse their holiday pay days and overtime. By that I mean, they will work unnecessary overtime on a holiday for 4.5x pay or whatever bs they get for being a manager with the power of overtime, and literally stand around asking housekeeping if there’s anything they can help with. They will walk around, cleaning something that was just cleaned by a houseman, and the housekeepers at the time could not be approved for any overtime. 

They also know ahead of time when the fire inspector is coming to inspect the hotel, which is a real shame, because the managers just make housekeeping clean up the storage rooms (ie moving flammable material away from the ceiling) for the inspection and then put it all back as a fire hazard as soon as the inspection is done.

They also believe the assistant managers over the “lesser employees” ie van driver and housekeeping. Once the assistant manager told a van driver to put some cleaning utensil down and help them with something. The van driver did, and then later they were chewed out by the manager for leaving hotel property unattended. Even though I was with the van driver and I vouched for the driver, the manager still believed the assistant manager over us, and the driver got a demerit on his record. I told them to check the cameras which would show the driver carrying the equipment and then getting waved over by the assistant manager and gestured to drop what the driver was carrying. They essentially told me to take a hike, and that the driver was SOL. 

Stay away at all costs. There’s a reason the other Marriott hotel got busted for having a drug cooking operation in the boiler room, just saying.           
By the way, when I gave my two weeks’ notice all the manager said was ‘ok.’ Didn’t even ask me why I was giving my notice or if there was anything they could improve on. No wonder the Residence Inn by Mariott Goleta has a huuuuge turnover rate for the cleaning staff, front desk, and drivers. 

Stay far, far away. People that reprehensible don’t change. Especially managers who get carried away with power.

Instead, leadership quickly combined my retirement announcement into an external event with about 30 customers. Because HR failed to notify the office internally, I had to send my own farewell email so my colleagues in the local office (on my last day with the company) would even know I was leaving. It feels like my decades of loyalty were used as a quick public relations talking point rather than being genuinely celebrated by the company.
