pros: Working at Dollar Tree provided valuable hands-on leadership experience across every aspect of retail operations. I strengthened my skills in inventory management, merchandising, freight planning, staffing, customer service, compliance, and operational execution. The fast-paced environment challenged me to think quickly, prioritize effectively, and develop my team while delivering results. The relationships I built with my associates and customers were by far the most rewarding part of the job.
cons: The workload often exceeded the labor hours provided, making it challenging to consistently meet operational expectations. Store managers were frequently expected to handle multiple responsibilities while working with lean staffing levels. Facility and equipment issues sometimes took longer than expected to resolve, and support from upper management could be inconsistent. While the job offered valuable experience, maintaining work-life balance could be difficult during peak freight and seasonal periods.
advice: Align expectations with the resources provided. When stores are expected to process large freight volumes, maintain recovery standards, and deliver excellent customer service, they need adequate staffing and labor hours to succeed. Listening to feedback from store-level leaders can help identify practical solutions and improve overall operations.

summary: Great Company but bad management
pros:
Food
Cab
Facilities
Team mates
Learning
cons:
The company itself is actually very good, and I would personally give it 10/10 in many respects. The 1-star rating is specifically because of my experience during the restructuring and internal team-transfer process.

I was part of 7-GT, which was dissolved, and employees had to move to other teams. For some reason, the other teams clearly did not like 7-GT and were reluctant to take people from the team. Because of organizational pressure, they eventually had to accept some of us.

What made the situation ridiculous was that employees were being subjected to 2–4 rounds of interviews just to move to another team within the same organization. This wasn't even for a client project, and there was no hike or salary increase involved. Employees were essentially being interrogated for the privilege of continuing their jobs in another internal team. If we were going to go through that much interviewing anyway, we could have simply interviewed elsewhere and potentially received a 35–60% hike.

During this period, junior employees, SE1s, SE2s, and leads were moved into different teams, while staff-level employees and architects were laid off. The entire process was extremely frustrating and demoralizing.

I personally interviewed with a team called Store Tech, under managers Subhadeep Mondal and Ankit. If your idea of an “Indian manager” is someone with zero respect, questionable technical knowledge, and an ego that is significantly larger than both, then these two are a perfect example.

My interview experience with them was terrible. They came across as arrogant, dismissive, and completely uninterested in listening to the candidate. It felt like they wanted to finish the interview as quickly as possible so they could get back to their tea break. Within the first 10 minutes, I was already 99% certain that I wouldn't be selected—not because of my answers, but because of the way they spoke to and treated me.

I answered approximately 90–95% of their questions correctly. At several points, they tried to convince me that my answers were wrong. I stuck to my answers, later verified them independently, and found that I had been correct.

Despite that, I was rejected approximately five minutes after the interview. I checked with HR and there was apparently no meaningful explanation for the rejection. It didn't even seem like there had been any serious discussion about my candidacy.

Later, after speaking with a few people from their team, I heard similar opinions about these two managers. Based on my own experience, I found them to be arrogant, disrespectful, and unpleasant people to deal with, and I remain baffled by how they ended up in management positions.

Ironically, getting rejected by them turned out to be one of the best things that happened to me. I interviewed elsewhere, received a 40% hike, and left the company.

Unfortunately, not everyone was that lucky. Some of my former colleagues were laid off.

And that's what makes the whole situation particularly frustrating. These managers had an opportunity to take capable employees into their team and potentially help them remain with the organization. Instead, people were rejected through an internal process that often felt arbitrary, while others ultimately lost their jobs.

So, congratulations to Subhadeep Mondal and Ankit: you rejected me, and that rejection helped me get a 40% hike somewhere else.

In hindsight, I should probably thank them.

As for their management style, though: massive ego, little respect, questionable technical depth, and absolutely no sense of how to treat people during an already stressful organizational restructuring. If they ever experience the other side of a layoff themselves, perhaps they'll finally understand what some of the employees they rejected and displaced went through.

Whoever hired them as managers—what exactly were you thinking?

On other note, there were lay off in the company around 12 people or so in 7-GT team alone. But it was step by step and it was not reported anywhere, I could not find anything in linkedinpost or in glassdoor by any of the employees, not sure with what they were threatened with.
advice:
Company should do reviews on Managers, are they capable or not. Most of the managers I met and worked with are 2/10. They believe they know stuffs, in fact all they know is how to smooth talk their superiors. 
Every 6 months an audit should be done on the so called Managers. 7-11 preaches certain principles but non of them are in effect in the organization when it comes to treating the employees.

summary: Results and culture are not separate lanes, they’re one strategy at Wawa.
pros:
What stands out most working for Wawa is how deeply Wawa lives its Six Core Values, especially Valuing People and Doing the Right Thing. The culture genuinely feels like one family, there’s a strong emphasis on respect, recognition, and caring for associates in meaningful ways, not just through words but through daily actions and company-wide programs. That consistency across stores and leaders is what makes the culture feel authentic and enduring. 
Teamwork is built into how we operate. From peer-to-peer recognition through Values nominations to servant leadership practices that encourage leaders to support and serve their teams, collaboration is reinforced daily. 
Leadership support at Wawa is rooted in servant leadership. Leaders are approachable, invested, and focused on helping you grow, not just driving results. There’s a strong balance between accountability and care, with access to coaching, mentorship, and resources that support both personal and professional development. 
Feeling valued comes from trust and recognition. Leaders are empowered to make decisions, develop their teams, and think like owners. Recognition programs, ongoing feedback, and visible investment in leadership development reinforce that store leaders play a critical role in the company’s success. 
Wawa provides continuous growth opportunities through leadership onboarding, formal training, hands-on learning, and movement between stores or regions. These experiences stretch your skills, broaden your perspective, and prepare you for the next level while keeping you challenged and engaged. 
I’m proud that Wawa is a company built around people, not just profits. Whether it’s how we treat our associates, serve our customers, or give back through The Wawa Foundation, there’s a clear commitment to making a positive difference in communities every day.

As a store operations leader, my role directly impacts Wawa’s mission of fulfilling lives every day. By developing strong teams, creating a welcoming environment, and delivering consistent customer experiences, I help bring that mission to life for both associates and customers. 

 If you are looking for a place where people matter, growth is encouraged, and hard work is recognized, Wawa is a great fit. It’s a fast-paced environment, but it’s also one where you’re supported, developed, and truly part of a team. 
Success in store operations comes from adaptability, strong communication, and a genuine commitment to serving others. Leaders who embrace Wawa’s values, stay open to feedback, and focus on developing their people tend to thrive and build strong, successful teams.
cons:
Store operations run 24/7, which can mean long and sometimes unpredictable work hours.
As a 24/7 operation, the role demands flexibility and long hours, especially during peak periods or high T/O staffing challenges.
advice: Focus on developing your people as intentionally as you manage the business; strong teams will always outperform strong managers working alone.

pros: High salary on paper and a car. The store assistants are absolutely amazing in spite of the terrible culture they need to operate in.
cons:
This was genuinely the most traumatising experience of my life. The impact this company has had long term on my self worth is astounding. They operate on a hierarchy built on who is the biggest bully all covered up by wearing posh suits. 

On my first day I was told I had to wear heels and couldn’t have a pink bag, I should’ve turned and ran at that point.

You start your day at 4am to drive to a store they’ve placed you in an hour from where you live. You won’t leave until maybe 9pm at night. I was falling asleep at the wheel to drive home. You will have no work life balance at all. You will work five days a week but on your days off you will be too depressed and tired to do anything.

I was shouted at for sending home a store worker who was crying on the tills because it ‘impacted the sickness KPI’. When I needed surgery I wasn’t able to have any days off and was too scared to ask for sick leave because ‘actions like this will stop you progressing on the graduate scheme’ so I ended up bleeding in the toilets in the store. 

I wish I could say I stormed out and had a final last word but instead they trained me to count stock from the office for speed and then accused me of committing fraud as front for asking me to resign when in actual fact they had hired too many graduates and needed to get rid of some.

I read reviews like this at the time and still chose to go for the job because I was flattered such a well respected scheme wanted me, I IMPLORE you not to do this. There is not a single graduate who started at the same time as me who is still on the scheme because they all get burnt out and realise the salary is not at all proportionate to the hours you work. All the graduates have had to retrain in something else at a significantly lower salary because this job give you no transferable skills (you are a glorified shop assistant). Save yourself some time and pick a scheme that will actually train you up, I promise you’ll make more money in the long run. 

If you do listen to this review - well done, Aldi really don’t deserve you.

If you read this and think ‘that won’t be me’ like I did then I really hope that is the case. As an aside, I found myself sitting reading the exact same Glassdoor reviews a year after I started wishing I’d listened so I’ll see you here in a year.
advice: Truly speechless, nothing will change because the issues flow right from the top. If you are a current Area Manager I advise you attend some external management courses to learn how to behave appropriately at work (and set you up well for your inevitable departure).

summary: Friendly environment overshadowed by poor upper management and false promises
pros: Friendly environment and great co-workers. Being a floral clerk was hands down my favorite customer service job I've worked. Made some nice friends working there, and the stress of work was easily handled because of the friendly people.
cons:
Seniority was definitely a thing. I was expected to take shifts that the other people didn't want until someone newer came along, and then I had seniority over them.

Upper management for the store was also the worst. They would take credit for our department's hard work and shift blame onto us for oversights or actions on their part. Once I got promoted to admin, I saw how little they cared about their employees. They would make passing comments and openly admit to giving certain employees who were "problem people" bad shifts or deny their requests for days off. I was in charge of making the schedule and would be told not to give certain people the days they wanted that week, even if they were within their availability, just to make things difficult for them.

They also don't promote from within. I was asked to be the interim manager when our manager went on maternity leave. I stepped up and took on manager duties despite not getting a pay raise. When my manager decided she wanted to move stores, she was hoping I would be given the role permanently. Instead, they decided to bring in someone from another store, and I had to train her to be a floral manager at ours.

They did eventually promote me to store admin, but my passion was working in floral. I agreed on the promotion as long as I could still work in the floral department, but they eventually phased me out of that role. Literally tricked me into taking a promotion and then falling back on the terms we agreed on.
advice: It doesn't take much out of your day to help people out. Maybe understand that everyone in the store is doing their best. Uplift your employees rather than make their time at work difficult, and these "problem people" might actually step up and help you out when you need.

understand this was more of a trust thing, but it hurt my efficiency and i would be looked at for not being fast enough]. summary: A horrific company rife with unethical practice
pros: There are none in my opinion
cons:
A company that claims to provide exceeding customer service in fact operates unethically, breaks promises, lies and adds extra pressure on already stretched staff. There’s a real sense of profit over people.

I joined as a management trainee confident I was joining a reputable company known for both its employee and customer satisfaction. From day one I realised that, having been “sold the dream” during the recruitment process, the reality was far from that promised.

I’ll start with the major issue: the unethical practice. The pressure on employees is enormous. Staff storages and high demand mean that overtime is commonplace. During the coronavirus pandemic, each car was supposed to be subject to the “Complete Clean Pledge”. In reality, to cope with demand, employees were “re-delivering” cars straight out to the next customer up to 3 times with no time to disinfect or clean them. My colleagues often broke speed limits (60 in a 30 zone, 40 mph in a 20 zone for example) in order to make deliveries on time and frequently used mobile phones whilst driving. One colleague told me that you “must drive like that if you want to make deliveries”. When I refused to adopt this so call “Management Trainee driving style” I was told to let other colleagues drive so that we could get the workload done on time. I refused, stuck to the speeds limits and left my phone on mute. This led one colleague to ask me “can you at least drive at a normal speed?”

Further unethical malpractice was renting out potentially dangerous vehicles. For example, Mercedes Benz issued a manufacture recall on their vans as a safety issue had been found with some models. The Enterprise computer system wouldn’t let these vans be rented so in order to get around this the shift manager selected a different car (be it a Vauxhall Insignia or Hyundai i10) on the system and gave the keys of the van to the customers regardless as sourcing another van would mean more work on for staff and dissatisfaction for the customers. 

Other issues are detailed below:

Being on the International Management Trainee Programme, at each interview during the recruitment process I was assured that the company would support my move to Spain by paying for my immigration documents and visa should I need one after Brexit. On the first day of the join I was informed “we do not sponsor visas”. I tried to contact the HR manager in London who was responsible for managing the International Programme but after several emails and missed calls I had no response. I was also supposed to be in contact with a representative in Spain however I like wise never heard a response from him. Also, the expenses incurred during the recruitment process took six months to be refunded and I only got them back after my local branch manager changed them on my behalf. 

With the promise of a career in Spain all but in tatters, the company’s response to the coronavirus pandemic was the last nail in the coffin. My manager proudly proclaimed in March that “all your jobs are safe and no one needs to worry about being made redundant” thanks to being a privately held company of the Taylor family. Flash forward a few months, I have been furloughed and every assistant manager in the Scotland Northern Ireland group had been made redundant or demoted. I only found this out through a colleague as the company provided no updates during my near 4 months of furlough. The same colleague told me that he wasn’t paid any overtime and had to argue with the area manager for time back in lieu.

When I returned from furlough, the PPE provided by the company was in adequate and social distancing impossible as we regularly spent prolonged periods of time in small cars with both colleagues and member of the public. At one stage I spend an afternoon crammed into a Merc A-class with four other colleagues.

The support from upper management was pitiful to say the least. During a staff consultation the General Manager told me, when I asked what measured were being put in place to provide PPE and up staff morale, “you shouldn’t be asking that type of question as I don’t have an answer at this stage.” Similar disregard was shown by my area manager who seemed so blind to the dissatisfaction of her staff and clearly held the attitude of profit over people at the expense of the health and safety of employees and customers. 

After large swathes of staff were made redundant demand continued to grow and the remaining staff were left grasping the keep the company going. Overtime became common place, regularly working up to 8pm with one branch still delivering cars at 11pm at night. The new recurring my branch was promised in order to reduce pressure were on two occasions sent to other branches instead. With plummeting staff morale my manager said to me at one stage that she would be surprised if any of us made it to the end of the month. Every management trainee I spoke to was wanting to leave and car journeys became just moaning about the company and talk of the new jobs we were all applying for. We were supposed to, as told during the recruitment process, spend approximately 50:50 time in the office and on the road. In reality up to 80% of the day was spend delivering or collect cars with only a few moments of break between driving.

Enterprise, contrary to its reputation and being in The Times Top 100 Graduate Employers list, is a disgusting company with little regard for its staff and customer safety where unethical practices are rife and profits are put ahead of everything else.
advice: Actually listen to the issues raised by your employees rather than justify them.

summary: Enterprise-London
pros:
Enterprise is a company where you control your progression and advancement .They reward hard work in  all aspects of the business.You get what you put in with Enterprise .Each customer transaction is your own to control ,weather it be finding the perfect car for that customer or advising them on certain products we offer .Within the company you get a taste for all different elements of the business such as customer service , sales , marketing , fleet growth  and much more .Enterprise is a fun and friendly place to work , the buzz is great and moral is always high .Sales and service games keeps everyone on their toes as well as keeping energy levels high at all times during a shift.Opportunities are endless in regards to career progression at Enterprise , you are a manager in training when join  Enterprise and your path is clearly laid out in front of you from day 1 .

Airport branches differ from city branches but both have their benefits.Day in each would consist of a morning meeting with all staff on shift that day.In the meeting managers and staff will discuss goals for the day,acknowledge positives from anyone present , delegate tasks and speak about reservations for the day.Throughout the day you will build rapport with customers and assist them throughout their rental agreement.In city and local branches you will get the opportunity to go and pick up customers and bring them to your branch (once your probation is up).Admin duties are completed throughout the day and consist of follow up calls,reservation confirmation and and issues customers may have with their rental.Before you know it your day is  done . 

On a personal note I joined Enterprise on a placement with University and loved every minute .I loved the teamwork , the working environment and opportunities that the company offered.I am now back at Enterprise picking up exactly where I left off and continuing my journey to becoming a manger.

So if you like a challenge , your driven ,your not afraid to roll your sleeves up now and again and your ambitious , Enterprise is 100 percent the place for you !
cons:
The hours at Enterprise can be challenging but as is with any customer service based roll in today's business environment .There is opportunity for overtime of course and is paid .

If you have not got any previous experience in customer service you may find it daunting at first but I assure you it is the best company to gain this experience from.

summary: Long Hours for Sissies, Just Right for me-Fun and Great Job
pros: Great for college grads that need to gain experience. The best thing about Enterprise is the environment. The really do promote their founding values and it is a fun place to work. Even though you often have to deal with customers that are not in the best mood, you have the support of you fellow employees and branch/area managers. Lot of potential for upward growth within the company if you work hard. It's has a real vibrant team work ethic. Great benefits including investment matching. Many of the people I have meet will be lifelong friends.
cons: Its not the best paying job in the world. They pay you hourly starting out and if your a family man then you have to make sure your hours are enough to cover your budget which means sometimes working extra weekends etc. Plenty of money if your single. Advancement is merit based but some areas have some inane requirements for promotion to Management which are based largely on luck and not skill. I have been told several times that I am ready for promotion but I can't be promoted because I do not fulfill all the requirements whereas people that are not as skilled get promoted because they do meet the requirements primarily for being in the right place and the right time.
advice: Better pay means better retention. Requirements for promotion are a good thing, they make people work harder in the beginning and help the company grow. However, most people only work hard to meet them and do not care too much after they have meet them. Allow for more flexibility with how can be promoted. There are several people that I work with that should be promoted but have not. Also, if you are doing all the work of a manager as an MT, you should get paid and promoted accordingly.

Have seen good people put in the does not meet expectations who are actually the smartest and team leads.  And what’s the reason for it?  Oh you are below on diff count for X amount of months, surely that means you’re slacking on your velocity.  Oh you only wrote on ERD over past couple months. pros:
High-Impact, Large-Scale Ownership: Working on systems, policies, or products that impact millions of users globally gives you immediate ownership and high visibility. Work moves fast and directly touches real-world operations.

Talented, Collaborative Peers: The cross-functional teams and individual contributors are usually driven, resourceful and provide unique perspectives. It’s an environment where you learn a lot simply by collaborating with smart people who know how to solve messy problems quickly.

Solid Employee Perks: Benefits like Uber credits, wellness stipends, and decent health, vision and dental insurance are above average.
cons:
Organizational Shifts & Job Insecurity: Fast-paced environments often come with frequent strategic pivots, restructuring, and reorgs. Priority shifts can make long-term project stability and role predictability difficult to maintain.

Regional Silos & Bureaucracy at Scale: As the company has grown, aligning global operations, policy, and engineering across different regions can sometimes lead to communication gaps, slow decision-making loops, or duplicated efforts.

Fast Pace Can Strain Work-Life Balance: The "bias for action" culture means expectations are high, and the boundary between work and personal time can blur—especially when collaborating across global time zones. Burnout is real.

Growth opportunities: Career progression can feel inconsistent. While growth opportunities exist, advancement often feels heavily dependent on managerial sponsorship rather than performance metrics alone, resulting in more lateral moves than upward promotion.

summary: Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.
pros: There is nothing good about lyft
cons: Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.
advice:
Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.

I originally booked an Uber, but I canceled it because I had a $10 Chase Sapphire ride credit that I wanted to use with Lyft.

When I booked my Lyft ride from my residence to Tampa International Airport, the app clearly showed the fare as $36.98. At that point, I hadn’t even entered my Chase Sapphire card information yet, so that quoted price could not have included the $10 Chase credit.

After I reserved the ride, Lyft placed a temporary authorization charge on my credit card for $36.98, confirming that this was the fare I had agreed to.

However, after the ride was completed, Lyft billed me $46.98. Only after the $10 Chase Sapphire credit was applied did my final out-of-pocket cost become $36.98—the exact price Lyft had displayed before I ever added my payment method.

In other words, the advertised fare wasn’t the actual fare at all. Lyft effectively increased the ride price by $10 and then used my Chase credit to bring it back down to the original quoted amount. That isn’t a discount—it’s misleading pricing that deprives customers of the benefit of their credit.

Displaying one price to get customers to book a ride and then charging a higher fare after the ride is completed is deceptive and undermines trust. If the actual fare is $46.98, that’s the price Lyft should display upfront. Customers shouldn’t discover after the fact that a third-party credit merely offsets an undisclosed price increase.

This experience has completely eroded my confidence in Lyft’s pricing transparency, and unless this billing practice changes, I won’t be using or recommending the service.

Another area for improvement is employee recognition. While mistakes and areas for improvement are frequently addressed, employees’ accomplishments and consistent hard work do not always receive the same level of acknowledgment. I also feel that compensation could be more competitive based on the responsibilities and expectations of the role.

Finally, opportunities for career advancement appear limited. During the hiring process, there was an expectation of growth and advancement, but in practice, those opportunities have not been clearly demonstrated. Providing employees with transparent career paths, development opportunities, and consistent recognition would greatly improve the overall employee experience.
advice: One recommendation for management would be to ensure that leaders receive thorough training and develop a strong understanding of the roles they are responsible for managing. This can lead to more effective communication, stronger support, better decision-making, and ultimately a more successful team.

advice:
★ 1 Star — DoorDash Completely Ignored a Serious App Problem and Penalized Me for It

I’ve completed nearly 5,000 deliveries as a Dasher and have maintained a 95%+ acceptance rate and Platinum Dasher status. I know how the DoorDash app is supposed to work, which makes what happened—and DoorDash’s complete lack of response—even more frustrating.

On July 28th, I started dashing and was hit with 15 timed-out orders. The problem? The assignments NEVER showed up on my phone. They didn't appear on my screen for me to accept or decline. I never saw the restaurants, the payout, the distance, or any other information about these orders. They simply weren't there.

I couldn't accept them. I couldn't decline them. I never even had the opportunity to make a decision because DoorDash never delivered the assignments to my phone.

And to be clear, this isn't a case of me using some outdated phone that can't handle the DoorDash app. I have a current, top-of-the-line smartphone with 5G capabilities, with more than enough capability to run the DoorDash app. I've completed nearly 5,000 deliveries using the platform.

I immediately contacted DoorDash multiple times and explained exactly what was happening. I was told they would investigate the issue. I actually stopped dashing for 10 days to give DoorDash time to figure out what was wrong before I tried again.

During those 10 days, all I received were generic, form-letter responses essentially saying, “Here's your reference number, and we're looking into it.”

Apparently, they weren't looking into anything.

On August 7th, I tried dashing again, and the exact same thing happened. This time I caught the problem after another 5 assignments timed out, bringing my total to 20 timed-out orders.

Twenty orders.

NONE of these were declined orders. I did not decline them. The assignments never showed up on my phone.

Some of these were high-paying orders. Some were very short, easy deliveries that I would have gladly accepted. I never even got the chance to see them.

Yet DoorDash's system apparently considers all 20 of these as though I intentionally chose not to accept them.

The result? My acceptance rate went from over 95% down to 76%, putting my Platinum Dasher status at risk.

I've contacted DoorDash repeatedly. I've explained the problem. I've given them the dates. I've provided the reference numbers. I've stopped dashing for 10 days while they supposedly investigated. Then I tried again and experienced the exact same technical failure.

And what has DoorDash done?

Nothing.

They refuse to properly investigate the technical problem. They refuse to correct the 20 timed-out assignments. They refuse to restore my acceptance rate. And they refuse to restore the Platinum status that I earned through thousands of deliveries.

After nearly 5,000 dashes, I know the difference between an order I intentionally decline and an order that never appears on my phone in the first place.

If DoorDash's system fails to deliver an assignment to a Dasher's phone, the Dasher should not be penalized for it.

I did everything I was supposed to do. I reported the problem. I stopped working for 10 days to give them time to investigate. I tried again, and the exact same problem happened. I've repeatedly contacted support, and instead of actually fixing the problem, I've been given generic responses and reference numbers.

At this point, I have no confidence that anyone at DoorDash is actually investigating my situation.

DoorDash needs to take responsibility for its own technology instead of making Dashers pay the price for technical failures that are completely outside of their control.

Nearly 5,000 deliveries, a top-of-the-line 5G phone, a history of maintaining a 95%+ acceptance rate, and Platinum status—and apparently none of that matters when their system fails and their support team refuses to fix it.

If you're considering becoming a Dasher, understand that when something goes wrong with the DoorDash app, you may be completely on your own.

Extremely disappointed in DoorDash and their support. One star is generous.

advice:
I'm frustrated by the hidden costs of dashing. The DoorDash app requires drivers to remain online for hours waiting for orders, consuming significant cellular data and draining phone batteries. Drivers are expected to provide and pay for their own phone, data plan, charger, maintenance, fuel, insurance, and vehicle expenses, yet there is no reimbursement for the mobile data used while simply waiting for orders that often never come. When you're sitting for hours without receiving worthwhile offers, those costs continue to add up while you're earning little or nothing.
DoorDash depends on Dashers to keep the platform running, but the current system places nearly all of the financial burden on drivers. I hope the company takes a closer look at the real costs Dashers absorb and makes meaningful changes to create a fairer and more sustainable experience.

Metrics were skyrocketed due to cheating (eg: from 14 to 22+ meetings ran/month), so now they’re very unlikely to be hit. Fast track program (promotion eligible after 11 months on phone) is notorious for producing egregious cheaters who eventually fail at AE. summary: Great at attracting talent, but the culture can push excellence out
pros: The brand, compensation, benefits, and flexibility are strong. The company attracts ambitious people and offers the chance to work on interesting, visible problems. There are also genuinely talented people who care about quality and want to build things that last.
cons:
The company is much better at attracting talent than it is at recognizing, developing, and retaining the people who actually raise the bar.

The values sound good, but they have not been turned into a consistent way of operating. Standards can change depending on the organization and who currently has influence. Culture often becomes whatever the most powerful person in the room rewards.

There is also a real gap between what people say privately and what they are willing to say when leadership is present. Someone may agree with a concern, support a recommendation, or make a commitment one on one, then take a different position in the next meeting. That makes trust difficult and teaches people to pay attention to politics before facts.

Too often, authority is treated as evidence. A confident story from a senior person can carry more weight than the actual work, the available data, or the judgment of people closest to the problem. The organization can accept a polished explanation without first checking what was delivered, what worked, who actually did the work, and what decisions or resources were missing.

When something goes badly, there is often more energy spent creating a clean explanation than understanding what really happened. The least politically disruptive story can win, while leadership decisions, unclear ownership, shifting priorities, weak sponsorship, and unresolved dependencies receive less scrutiny. This protects the existing power structure, but it also means the organization does not learn much from failure.

There is a lot of bureaucracy without enough discipline. Calendars are packed with meetings, reviews, working groups, and status updates, but many of those conversations do not end with a clear decision, owner, or deadline. The same issue can move through multiple forums while everyone appears busy and aligned.

Teams can also spend more time pursuing their own agendas than solving the shared problem. The company often looks coordinated from the outside, but inside there can be little agreement on who owns the complete outcome. This creates activity without much cohesion.

Career growth does not consistently feel merit based. Strong judgment, sustained delivery, deep expertise, and the ability to improve quality do not always lead to greater opportunity or influence. Visibility, proximity to leadership, and support for the preferred narrative can matter more.

Ownership also becomes less clear once work gains attention. Something created by an individual or team can be renamed, redirected, or absorbed into a more senior leader’s story. The original builders may continue carrying responsibility while losing credit, authority, or influence over what happens next.

Repeated external hiring adds to the problem. New leaders are often brought in from whichever company, industry, or technology is currently viewed as the next big thing. Outside experience can be valuable, but recognizable company names are sometimes treated as proof that someone will be successful here.

The pattern becomes repetitive. A new leader arrives with a new vocabulary, new relationships, and a new organizational design. Existing work is redirected or devalued. Internal people who already understand the problem are overlooked. Before the company has learned whether the new approach worked, another change begins.

This is not the same as raising the bar. Real bar raisers make the work better, make the people around them better, develop talent, give credit honestly, and leave behind something that continues to work. A senior title, polished communication style, or famous previous employer is not the same thing.

The culture can instead reward people who are good at looking successful. Managing upward, attaching yourself to visible work, protecting your position, and staying close to current leadership can be safer than challenging weak reasoning or demanding higher-quality execution.

That creates an every-person-for-themselves environment. Collaboration is discussed constantly, but people learn to protect their relationships, visibility, scope, and credit. Managers may be supportive in private while being unwilling to spend political capital when their teams actually need advocacy.

The biggest long-term risk is not simply losing institutional knowledge. It is losing people who genuinely care about doing excellent work.

Those people want high standards, honest feedback, fair credit, strong teammates, and a clear relationship between contribution and opportunity. They do not want to spend as much energy defending ownership and navigating politics as they spend doing the work. Eventually, many of them will choose an environment where quality and integrity are more clearly valued.

The company can therefore continue hiring impressive people while becoming less excellent. The people most willing to challenge mediocrity select out, while the behaviors that protect mediocrity become more deeply embedded.

The remote policy is also more equitable on paper than in practice. Important context, senior access, sponsorship, and relationship building still tend to center around the Bay Area. Employees elsewhere can be included in meetings while remaining at a real disadvantage in visibility and influence.
advice: Turn the stated values into an actual operating standard by putting evidence above rank, assigning accountability to the people with real authority, protecting accurate ownership and credit, and judging leaders by what they build, whom they develop, and what remains after they move on. Then look honestly at who has left over the last year and determine whether the company is retaining genuine bar raisers or rewarding people who are simply better at looking like them

summary: Exciting challenges in a mission-driven engineering culture
pros: Airbnb's mission of creating a world where anyone can belong anywhere strongly resonates with me. I'm excited by the opportunity to build products that operate at global scale and directly impact millions of users. My background in full-stack engineering, distributed systems, cloud infrastructure, and AI-powered applications aligns well with Airbnb's focus on innovation, reliability, and exceptional user experiences. I am particularly attracted to Airbnb's engineering culture, emphasis on ownership, and commitment to solving complex technical challenges while delivering meaningful value to hosts, guests, and communities worldwide.
cons: One challenge of working at Airbnb is the complexity that comes with operating a global platform at scale. The company culture has changed a lot and is definitely not the same as it used to be. At the same time, many new positions are being created in other regions, especially in the U.S. and India, leaving limited growth opportunities for employees in Canada.

summary: Airbnb: Good, Bad, and Mostly Ugly
pros:
- Friendly and inviting environment

cons:
- Poor training (gaps exist in workflows, workflows are tailored to senior agents only and not new joiners)
- Metrics (discussed briefly, but never something emphasized until it's too late) 
- Low pay (you're criminally being underpaid for this role and it's responsibilities despite the company being massive)
- False expectations (be okay with metrics that were closed to meeting, but suddenly, cutting you loose without any advance notice)
advice:
I appreciated the welcoming team environment and autonomy in this role. Those are genuine strengths. However, I want to surface three systemic issues that directly impacted my ability to succeed at Airbnb and will likely affect future hires:

1. Training & Workflows: Onboarding covered basics, but critical workflows were either missing or tailored to senior agent expectations. New hires faced a gap between training and actual case complexity. Recommend: detailed SOPs, tiered workflow documentation, and structured knowledge checks before agents work independently. This is key and basic.

2. Metrics & Expectations: Metrics weren't clearly weighted or explained upfront. Performance felt acceptable through the first 6 months, but the criteria for contract continuation were never explicitly discussed. This created misalignment and left no room for course correction. Recommend: transparent KPI thresholds from day one, warning of outcomes if KPI's are not met and early flagging if performance is off-track.

3. Compensation: Pay was below-market for the skill level and scope required, especially given the company's scale. This likely drives turnover and makes it hard to attract strong talent. Recommend: competitive market analysis and adjustment for the role's complexity or simply stop hiring contractors. Choose a lane.

These aren't personal issues—they're structural. Fixing them will improve retention and performance across the team. I'm happy to discuss further.

summary: Speed Over Rigor - Concerns About Sustainability and Governance
pros: There are talented individuals across the organization and strong ambition around innovation. The pace is fast, and leadership encourages bold execution.
cons:
In my experience, strategic emphasis increasingly prioritized speed and market positioning over operational rigor. Rapid initiatives were launched with urgency, sometimes without sufficient time for validation, auditability, or long-term sustainability planning.

Discussions around data governance, reporting assumptions, and structural safeguards did not always receive proportional attention relative to go-to-market velocity. This created internal tension for teams responsible for execution and compliance considerations.

The pressure to move quickly sometimes outweighed thoughtful risk assessment. Individuals who raised structural concerns did not always feel supported in slowing down initiatives to ensure stability and data integrity.

As a contractor, navigating these dynamics felt particularly challenging due to limited influence over strategic direction combined with high accountability for outcomes.

Over time, this created an environment that felt reactive rather than deliberate, with morale impacted by shifting priorities and execution reversals.
advice: Balance innovation velocity with governance, auditability, and long-term infrastructure stability. Encourage open dialogue around risk without framing it as resistance to progress.

summary: Progressively getting worse every day
pros:
* Great salary
* Nice compensation package
* Work from anywhere
cons:
* Management has progressively been getting more top-down, with few ways to offer your opinion (and it won't get listened to anyway)
* Related to above, all the AI talk in the media comes from management. We are mandated to use Claude code, people pushing for AI in coding got promoted to staff and principal over that, no actual effort to evaluate it as a tool. They even started measuring number of PRs people open and how long it takes to review a PR as a metric, something the industry knew is a terrible metric since the 80s. It used to be teams had autonomy in deciding which tools to use, but there were guides, recommendations and approved tooling (from a security perspective)
* Slack history is deleted because Management got pissy about the leaks. Given how important Slack is to everyday work this was a massive loss of company knowledge base. It was apparent before that Management has no idea what day to day of an average worker looks like with how much they were pushing Workplace (before Meta killed it), but had little to no Slack presence
* If upper management reports a bug with the app, you have to drop everything to fix it. Insanely disruptive, no changes to the behavior after many, many complaints through different formats about it
* Used to claim transparency and "no office politics" as part of the culture, but then studios get killed over office politics and any transparency efforts are curbed by all the other policies
* Stealth layoffs - they got smarter after the first big round of layoffs where 10% of the company got fired and morale fell, now they do a bunch of smaller layoffs and "reorgs" in different areas to make it less obvious
advice:
Engage with employee feedback. The disconnect between what the upper management thinks an average workday looks like and what it actually is grows by the day. Tools we actually use are ignored and we are pushed to use tools many dislike. 
We are not an AI company. We are just the consumers of AI products. We won't get any more efficient using AI tools as our bottlenecks are in different areas. Promoting sycophants will backfire. 
We are also a company who's two main competitors have a massive tech advantage over us and also have in-house AI tools. This is not a race we should be engaging in the first place, we are in a great position to wait and see what the future of AI looks like.

summary: The epitome of the phrase “You don’t quit jobs, you quit managers”. I don’t recommend
pros: While I am rating this job as a 1-star, there were a couple of good things, but the cons heavily outweigh these pros. So, I do want to be fair and completely transparent by mentioning everything, good and bad.  First of all, I loved the people who worked for me as their Unit Manager, which is the industry equivalent to a general manager of a single store. I cared about them and they cared about me. During training I worked at multiple stores and I witnessed that from from each store. Show that you genuinely care about them and they will care about you. I also loved my customers, especially the regulars; as they become part of your every day life. You work 6 days on and 1 day off. So your day off is not the same every week. You get 3, 10 day vacations a year. Fair warning about that though. They make you take those 10 days all at once. There’s no using one day here and another day there. So be prepared for that. I was an outside hire, but they do like to promote from within when people are qualified and interested. The highest level of management are visible, and if you work there long enough, you will probably meet the CEO. I thought that was pretty neat, and I’ve only ever experienced that in one other company I worked for in the past.
cons:
Now onto the cons. You work each and every holiday. You will never have one off. If you call off, you will most likely not have a job afterwards. In fairness, they warn you about that when you’re getting hired. 

You work 6 days a week, 6am to 2pm (don’t always expect to get out on time though). What they don’t tell you is that twice a week, you are expected to come in on the evening shift and count the money in the unit. This basically makes two of your evenings completely ruined and you cannot make plans on these days after work. So your already strained work-life balance is even more strained due to this. This is something they do not warn you about ahead of time.

Another thing they don’t tell you about. There will be “bonding” events with your fellow managers in the districts. This would be fine on an irregular basis, but they happen often enough to be disruptive to your life. They were mandatory to attend, even on your day off. So that’s another evening or day off you have to devote to this company instead of yourself or your family. 

Now onto management. As I said in the title, you don’t quit your job, you quit your managers. My district manager was great. He was my direct boss and oversaw multiple stores. His supervisors, the division manager, is the level of management where I saw the most problems. Having seen multiple division managers, the behavior was the same with all of them. That’s where they start caring about profit more than people. One example is where I discovered that the division manager did something to my store in order to fix a problem that we had been having. When I came in the next day, I saw the patchwork job and thought that it was a dangerous fix that could possibly bring harm to people. It was a fix that was very visible to the customers who also brought up concerns to me. I gave the benefit of the doubt to the division manager who made the fix, as I figured he simply made the fix in good faith and was ignorant to the danger, as well as the legal implications. When I brought up the concern to him, I was told “I’ve done it before, and it’s only illegal if you get caught”. I told them that I was uncomfortable being put in this situation. I was informed that they didn’t care, as the proper fix was too expensive. I did end up going to the legal authorities who did agree with me. They told me if they had discovered the issue themselves, that they would have shut the store down and taken legal action. But since I was the one who brought it to their attention and they hadn’t discovered it themselves on a random audit, that they would allow a short grace period to get the proper fix done. So, Waffle House magically found the money to get it fixed. 

After this, I was treated extremely poorly. I was told that I was directly responsible for my unit being over budget due to the fix, and that I should have kept my mouth shut and waited for the next fiscal year when it would not have affected the district as much. 

I did end up talking to the district manager’s boss at one point. He talked to me for over an hour and seemed to genuinely care and actually said they agreed with me. The problem was, nothing was done about the inherent issue and I was still treated poorly by the division manager. 

Lastly, I ended up going to the state labor department, specifically the whistleblower department. They agreed with my actions and told me to document absolutely everything, and that if any retaliatory actions happened, that they would take legal action against the company on my behalf. It was only after I informed the company that I did this that the poor treatment stopped.

Thankfully, no legal action ever needed to be taken as I left the company shortly after and I didn’t need to find out. 

I may sound like a disgruntled ex-employee, which is why I wanted to address the good things in detail as well. Waffle House’s mission and core values are great, but when the highest level of management do not project those values, it ruins the experience for everyone else, and you will not keep a good employee. I was dedicated to this company, my staff, and my customers. But Waffle House was not dedicated to me, and in the end, I left because of that.
advice: Management, care about your people. Practice what you preach, and you will be a great company. I hope my issues were isolated, but you need to address these things properly when they happen. If you don’t know these things are happening, that’s fine, but address it when it’s brought to your attention. I miss a lot about the place, specifically the family atmosphere I had at my store. However, management sets the tone, and I was left disappointed.

summary: Easy to learn. Exhausting. Abysmal corporate policies.
pros:
1. The job is incredibly easy to pick up. Be nice to guests, be patient, help out other servers, and just be a nice person. Boom. That's it. 
2. The other employees, and even some managers are genuinely amazing. I like all the managers I work with, but I could also just be lucky. 9/10 of the workers are wonderful people and are the only reason (that isn't money, obviously) that I still work here. Without them, I'd have quit because the exhaustion would've turned me into a Japanese salaryman.
3. The scheduling, at least for me, is incredibly lenient. Especially for students, people with other jobs, parents, etc. You'll more than likely have a schedule that works for you. Plus, you can even just be off schedule and pick up unwanted or offered shifts. Super super flexible.
4. No tax on tips I guess, which is 99% of the money you'll be making here.
cons:
Where do I even begin, by golly. I encourage you to read through it all, but I left a short paragraph in the botton explaining the gist of my grievances.

1. Corporate policies will actively hinder our chances of having good shifts. On top of having 0 breaks, we'll have at least 1 section of sidework assigned and 100 rolls of silverware to prepare. I have no problems with rolling silverware and having mandated sidework, but there's often just not enough time to do it and leave on time. Every time I find out about a new policy, it's just a way to make our jobs more insufferable. For example, finding out I had to portion at least either 12 or 24 cups of every condiment for secondary  because I had to constantly stop to deal with tables (and on top of that, whoever had the station last didn't maintain it properly and we were out of lots of condiments, so I had to restock it in its entirety by myself). For another example, we have slips we're required to fill out during our shift with friendly reminders to upsell and requiring us to go on little scavenger hunts to get people to check and sign our assignments. The slip itself and the papers they post of our beverage sale percentage reek of desperation from a company that would gleefully pay us literally nothing if a new law dissolved the federal subminimum wage.
2. There is a massive disconnect between what corporate wants, and what the guests want. The guests want good food and free bread that isn't frozen and reheated overnight. Corporate wants us to script a bunch of nonsense and have us act like used car salesmen. The guests are the ones who pay my bills and decide whether or not I deserve to eat. I'm going to act in their interests, not the company giving me $18~20 weekly. 
3. Some of the guests make me want to throw the decorations from the wall through the window. There's no shortage of creepy old men that regular at cracker barrels and will only tip female employees. Guests also frequently just... do whatever they want like sitting wherever and walking inside the nooks between the kitchen and dining rooms. Plus, you have to enable their behavior because making them upset means you don't get paid. It really sucks being disrespected and not being able to do anything about it because you rely on them to pay you.
3⅓. No forced gratuity for large parties means a large group can waste at least an hour of your time and take up most, if not all your tables, with absolutely 0 compensation. And it happens to everyone. 
3⅔. I have never seen a male server get a $50+ tip, but near enough every female server I've worked with (that do morning shifts) has gotten at least a $100 tip. If you're a woman, you're just more likely to get paid more. Men can still get good money, but women are far more likely to succeed here.  
4. The time you're scheduled to leave will almost never be the time you leave unless you have something worked out with management to be an exception. Because of the amount of side work you'll have to do, plus the fact you can get sat a table AT the time you're scheduled to leave is ludicrous. I can't plan anything on days I have morning shifts.
5. They love having 1~3 hour windows with no hosts, to-go, and like 1, maybe 2, person /people on the line. This means we'll have to stretch ourselves thin during a time we could be rolling 1/100 mandated rolls of silverware per server, or doing our sidework to do the jobs of hosts/to-go's, who'd otherwise earn 4.5x/7x our wage.
6. Cracker barrel refuses to hire anything but servers. Just this month I've seen 2 servers learn other roles because of the abundance of servers gutting their hours. We desperately need more grill cooks and dishwashers, but no instead we have 2 new servers training on the same day. Because we surely didn't have enough of those.
7. Even though any location will likely have too many servers, working a morning and afternoon shift in the same day isn't rare. Coupled with my issues expressed in statement 4, and I'm pretty dang sure I'm not being overdramatic when I say that I hate waking up on these days.

To kind of sum it up, servers are paid nothing and expected to do everything. Corporate policies consistently make our jobs more insufferable and dampen the guests' experiences. Guests can be the worst people on the planet to you, but you have to suck it up to maybe get paid by them. It's not guaranteed.
advice: There are way too many random rule changes with 0 notice. There should be announcements whenever something changes so that everyone is on board. For example, the new slips that you need to fill out during your shift, or changes to how sidework needs to be handled. This should be announced to all employees in a group chat or by email so that we can be well informed in case we were not present during the date of the change.

summary: Poor leadership and inconsistent workplace environment
pros:
Most coworkers were genuinely great to work with and made shifts more enjoyable.
* The guest interaction and serving aspect of the job is something I personally enjoy.
* Some shifts could be positive depending on staffing and team on duty.
cons:
*Management was often unprofessional with inconsistent communication and expectations.
* Certain coworker behavior occasionally affected morale and created a less positive work environment.
* There was a noticeable blame culture where issues were not handled in a constructive way.
* In my experience, bringing up workplace concerns or uncomfortable situations did not always feel welcomed or supported, and it sometimes felt like speaking up led to negative attention.
* Scheduling and hours were inconsistent, making it hard to rely on stable income.
*     Inconsistent scheduling sometimes resulted in difficult shift patterns, including working split doubles (such as 9–3 followed by a 4–close shift), which often meant not getting out until around 10:30 PM and then repeating the pattern on consecutive days.
* Training was limited, and expectations were often unclear, which made the job more stressful than it needed to be.
*     In my experience, HR concerns or formal complaints did not feel like they were taken seriously or addressed in a meaningful way.
advice: Implement a clearer and more accessible “open door” policy so employees feel comfortable reporting concerns without fear of backlash. Complaints should be handled in a transparent and consistent way so staff feel heard and taken seriously. Management should also be held to the same accountability and standards as hourly employees to create a fair and respectful work environment.

summary: Started Off Great! Until Management Went Downhill…
pros:
^Beginning^*2022*

***VERY friendly staff/coworkers. It was welcoming and everyone would help each other/fill positions on the clock if one of us needed any help. Always had lots to talk about and generally was just a very supportive work environment. 

***Management was very fun to work with and weren’t stingy at all with discounts/free meals. If we were hungry at break we were encouraged to eat a good meal.. even if we weren’t hungry then we still were encouraged to have food made before leaving for the day after our shifts. Very patient and solution oriented.

***Very flexible schedules and understanding of outside influences and engagements or sick days if we couldn’t come in.

***Workload and compensation was fair enough, but honestly the pay could’ve been a bit higher, maybe $14 or $15 instead of 11, but wasn’t terrible.

(2022- mid 2023)
cons:
^End^*2025*

***Employees that had basically been Panera veterans had started leaving to find new work (not all, but most), so the people I was left with hardly conversed with me, and if they did it was rather awkward so a majority of the time it was just us bringing items to each other or communicating about orders. Nothing inherently wrong with that, but I prefer work environments that are always inviting and are like a small family, which wasn’t this.. very stagnant (..and slightly performative)

***Apparently, the benefits/food discounts have been cut, which may be a corporate issue, but this isn’t a good look for the company with nearly minimum wage. It’s baffling how bad the greed gets when you have to chop down the discount for overpriced food… 

***Which leads me into my next point— The food and service quality has gone down SIGNIFICANTLY. I don’t understand how it’s so hard to remember BACON on a BACON Mac n Cheese?… or the wet wilting greens/lettuce they started using on food. These are just a few examples of how they don’t pay attention and/or are too careless about their job. These are recurring issues, this food quality, and I would ÑØȚ be surprised if they get in trouble for health code violations. Management talks big talk about store cleanliness and customer satisfaction, but they don’t actively do anything to remedy the issues or up the quality..

***Speaking of Management!
MY BIGGEST COMPLAINT, which is about MY former location, I can’t speak for all of them— is the management. One manager specifically I will not name, is so performative, and management as a whole doesn’t care about anything except making themselves look good and gaining clout (at an overpriced fast food cafe, mind you). They were extremely performative and force themselves to plaster a fake smile to employees and customers alike, and especially at those they do not care for. I’ve seen it in action. It really is something for a MANAGER to feel the need to COMPETE with an EMPLOYEE who is simply doing their job and interacting authentically with customers and coworkers, and campaign against them to other coworkers behind your back while plastering an uncanny smile at you to your face. Extreme toxicity wrapped in a care package. 

I ^wouldn’t^ recommend this job, at least not at this location, but if this is your only option, stand up for yourself while you’re there and know your worth. I wish I had. <3
advice: You know who you are. Get your act together. You’re not inviting or quirky, you’re a try hard. Do better. :)
